title: [AoS] Competitive Innovations in the Mortal Realms: 2026-11-25
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

After a couple weeks of 1-2 events, we got a solid 4 events week of mid-size, from the US, to the UK and even up to Sweden.

This Week's Events

  • Renegade Open 2026 - AoS GT - United States
  • Realmshift Series 2026 - Chapter 3 - United Kingdom
  • The Standoff 2026 AoS - United States
  • Fantasia Fanatic L Age of Sigmar - Sweden

Thoughts

Awakened Wyldwoods are going to be a serious pain in the ass for a Pyregheist, hiding in the woods until the time is right to strike. While Nighthaunt have way more guys to capture objectives with, Sylvaneth get to play the long game. Strike out with Kurnoths, Alarielle and Spiteriders, then hide back in the trees until they are sufficiently weakened to secure victory.

Nighthaunt usually win by playing objectives or battle tactics, not brute strength, as they lack some serious hard hitting units like other armies do. But Sylvaneth can almost patch them pound for pound in movement and that's going to be a real tough challenge to keep up with.

Result

Sylvaneth Victory - 68 - 46

Daniel Dowell - Sylvaneth - 1st Place

Branchwych. Credit: Rockfish

The List

See Showdown

Archetype

Alarielle and Kurnoths

Thoughts

With this list you have some decent flexibility with being able to remain back in your trees and hold your ground while also being able to strike out. Sylvaneth is an army that plays the long game, playing conservatively as their Overgrowth spreads out so they can better control the board in the second half of the game. With Spiteriders, you can fly out, charge and destroy a unit and then leave at the end of turn, allowing you to weaken the enemy before they come into your treeline where the Kurnoths and Alarielle beat them senseless. Spite-revenants are annoying enough, and cheap enough, to put them on objectives to capture them. Even if they die shortly after, they did their job.

Tzeentch generally is an army that's trying to play to objectives rather than raw strength. Their ability to teleport, swap out units, and generally move rapidly around the battlefield while miring their opponents in tarpits while they chuck mortal wounds at them makes them very frustrating.

Pretty much everything in the list works to serve this goal, Horrors are a tarpit with a Lord of Change making them -1 to be hit, slinging out mortal wounds with spells and even bringing back more to do it all over again. If you do need a hammer to swing into things, you got the Tzaangor Enlightened and Daemon Prince, swap them out of reserve and surprise your foes!

title: MTG Star Trek card sees 220% price spike, despite making Borg decks actively worse
content:
This new MTG price spike is more interesting than most. Death Is Irrelevant has risen from $5.50 to $17.50 since Star Trek's launch, a significant bump of 219%. It's risen for one simple reason: Commander players are loving those Borg-y Borg, with the Borg Queen being the most popular of the four precon face commanders by far. The intriguing part though, is that - at least in my opinion - Death Is Irrelevant has no business being in a 'We Are The Borg' deck.

Don't get me wrong, it's a fantastic card. I defied the set review guides that had this ranked low and absolutely cleaned up with it in Draft, even getting to steal a Benedict Cumberbatch Sheoldred in one particularly memorable match. If Death Is Irrelevant is in play, you're laughing, stealing the best creature each turn while your entire army becomes unkillable.

But it is an eight mana enchantment which is only really worth the mana if it sticks around for multiple turn cycles. We Are The Borg already struggles with card costs, laboring under a seven mana commander. Your top end is sorted - a large part of it is the queen herself. What the deck really needs is more early game presence and interaction.

It doesn't need a massive enchantment card like this. It has no way of cheating it into play, and since lots of its ramp cards only work with artifacts, a lot of the time it won't be able to cast it. There's a very real risk of this rotting in your hand till you're beaten.

But, just like the Borg Cube price spike I covered earlier in the week, what Death Is Irrelevant has going for it is it leans into the fantasy players want to fulfill - of being an unstoppable Borg menace.

Also, it assimilates, I'm seeing that a lot of people really want more of the assimilate mechanic, a super thematic form of card theft, far more than generic artifact synergies. Which could also help explain why both this and Borg Cube have spiked hard in price despite not necessarily being the most optimal inclusions.

I wouldn't expect Borg players to be so easily led by their emotions, though that said I would be right there with you throwing these cards into the list if I was building these decks (and if they hadn't both gotten much pricier). Who cares about what's strongest? What's fun is much more important.

For more stories and chat join the Wargamer Discord, and if you like learning about money in Magic, check out our list of the most expensive MTG cards.

title: Magic: The Gathering Puzzlebox – Building the H.M.S. Bounty on a Budget
content:
If I had a nickel for every Monoblue Commander that saw essentially zero hype during spoiler season that I intended to break and elevate in the months following, I'd have...what, three nickels now? Four, I suppose, but Eluge was always destined to succeed. Following in the footsteps of Princess Yue, Immortus, and the gar himself, my recent fascination has been with the H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship, from the communuity-maligned Star Trek set. Excitement for this card was low on release, including my own skepticism, but after having played over a dozen online games, and two FNMs' worth with the ship, I must confess that this is the coolest Commander I've gotten to play in some time. While the Bounty looks janky, the pool of Whales is shockingly deep, and the combos it enables are backed up with one of the best enablers for a tutor Commander of all time, Dreamtide Whale. There's one problem—if you wanted to buy the list I covered in a cool ~4k words without proxying (which I highly encourage), it would run you around $2,500. For playgroups without proxies, or for those otherwise preferring genuine cardboard, that's untenable; for this reason, I made it my goal to shave down the price of this fantastic Commander and make it accessible to everyone, proxies or not. You can build a compelling, competent, and frankly sweet version of the Bounty for $60, and still sail the stars with your cetacean companions pretty darn well. Let's dive into it.

This is part of a shortform Magic series where I’m covering rapid-fire concepts about Commander that I couldn’t cover in a full Commander Focus, so if you like what you see, certainly let us know!

Whale-Watching on a Budget

Before we get into the weeds, it's worth familiarizing ourselves with the Bounty's core gameplan, which I covered in the primer here. The deck has a three-pronged gameplan, where we aim to find Steelfin Whale and a Knack effect (the fastest win, but requires that it stick or have Haste), Orvar & Great Whale alongside Mind Games (slower, and requires Lands that tap for 5+, but doesn't need Haste), or Luxior, Giada's Gift with a Commander stationed to 18 (functionally 21 Commander Damage). Slight problem there—Great Whale spiked to ~$180 after it was revealed Whales would be included in 'Sea Monster' bucket post-Nauctis, and as a Reserve List card its supply is limited. So, that takes out Plan B, leaving us to be more reliant on Steelfin lines for combo wins, and more reliant on Luxior for fair wins. Another problem that crops up, however, is that Steelfin lines require mana rocks that go mana-positive as a target to bounce and recast, which are a huge reason as to why the budgetless list is so expensive. Things like Moxen and even Grim Monolith are hugely important for your endgame, and those cost a pretty penny. On a budget, the only mana rock that goes positive is Sol Ring, but thankfully it's fairly findable. Once you pare away the combo pieces & mana-positive rocks, what more does the Bounty need? Well, blink helps us protect our pieces and re-tutor, and utility Creatures help us gain advantage over time and station up our Commander alongside Dreamtide Whale. We can take that schema of wincons, blink, and value Creatures, and transfer it to the budget version pretty cleanly!

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

There are some pretty easy swaps, such as Faerie Mastermind being exchanged for Ghostly Pilferer, or Reshape being taken out for Scour for Scrap, but where things get interesting is in the expansion of aspects of our gameplan which aren't fast enough for the budgetless version. Take for example Moxite Refinery, which is sort of a second Luxior, able to turn Charge counters into +1/+1 counters, similarly resulting in combat damage wins. It's a bit more awkward to use than Luxior, but it's also dirt cheap, and does a well enough job when it comes to abusing the fact that our Commander is a Spacecraft. In much the same way, Leyline of Transformation makes everything into Whales, so our Commander becomes a strict Creature tutor in the Command Zone, which helps us play like more of a toolbox and even find Knack effects by chaining through Micromancer. We're even playing Kaho, Minamo Historian alongside Hidden Strings, which can in theory find the entire Steelfin win on its own if we have sufficient mana, by untapping Kaho twice via the Cipher and an unblocked Creature (such as our Flying Commander). Finally, this list is uniquely on a Speed package, with highlights like the Raceways, Vnwxt, Verbose Host, and Racer's Scoreboard. This is in service of having another Haste enabler—Amonkhet Raceway—but the fact our Commander gives us an Extra Turn means that we can hit max speed faster than most decks, which lets us get a ton out of the mechanic! Again, this is assisted by the Start Your Engines! cards being pennies on the dollar.

Dream Big, Dreamtide

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

At time of writing, this list comes in at a cool $59.56, which is ~$15 less than the Borg precon that's come out from the same set, and certainly more powerful. I think there's something telling about the fact that the two most expensive cards in the list are Dreamtide, your first tutor target 99% of the time, and Luxior, a wincon. This is a list running on pretty slim margins, but the strength of a tutor in the Command Zone and what is essentially a guaranteed Extra Turn once per game really does earn its keep in spite of that; when there's a limiting factor on a deck, be it because of its status as a precon, budget, or some other theme, concentrating the power in the one card you know you have access to is a pretty safe bet. This list is currently built as Bracket 2, where the budgetless thrives at the high end of Bracket 3, but you could honestly toss a couple moxen in here and pitch it as the fabled 'Game Changer-less 3', aka Bracket 2.5. The upgrade paths are pretty clear, which does a lot to help this serve as a deck you can keep in its budget state, or slowly build towards something more optimized.

Decklists are kept updated, and may change with set releases.

I think it is worth interrogating why the Bounty has me so smitten, because frankly I'm surprised that it's already become the Bracket 3 deck I'll reach for when that's the power the pod asks for, so much so that I've unironically considered keeping the budget version with me as well just to get more Bounty games in. There's a few objective truths of the card: Having a limited tutor means you get a toolbox, but nothing too broad or obvious, and taking an Extra Turn is strong enough that chaining them is verboten by writ of the Bracket system. It manages to do two of the most powerful things in Commander—tutoring and turns—but neither in such a way that you get out too far ahead, or break the social code of the format. You brush against it, yes, but those lines go uncrossed, and as a Johnny/Spike that has a certain appeal. More than that though is the fact the Whales which exist in Magic are such that you have everything from value plays to combos at your disposal, and moreover, multiple combos enabled by, and using outlets via, Whales. It's such an absurd statement to say that this type which has existed since Narwhal in 1995's Homelands, having received no support up to this point, randomly has the exact tools it needs to both produce infinite mana readily, and expend it just the same.

Subjectively, that's the coolest facet of the card, right alongside the fact you need to work a bit to actually turn it on (via Stationing), but the first thing you tutor can in theory get you to 8 Charge counters the turn after. Whales form this esoteric sort-of archetype, and coming from a Yugioh background, the searching and semi-linear play pattern really appeal to my sensibilities. I would wager they'll appeal to you too, dear reader, and for a cool $60 you can get your fins on the coolest deck I've built since Yue. I think my only real concern is that Whales receive enough support in Nauctis that this becomes too known, or well-supported, and it loses the contrarian appeal I am cursed to bear. Suffering from success. I suppose. For anyone without that particular brainworm, however, this deck has much to look forwards to in the coming months, and I suspect building it now while the Whales not on the Reserve List are inexpensive is likely a wise choice.

title: Lenoon’s Warhound: Joy
content:
I should start with a confession. The whole point here was to journey together into process. To talk to artists, visionaries, geniuses, the creative and the profound (and ideally the infinite and the divine, not to mention the wicked and the warped), but then life took over and the Warhound built its own momentum, charging forward as the calendar ticked on and on. The discussions were the best bit, so when I could, I talked. Everyone I talked to - from passing chats to proper interviews - was interesting, fascinating people with valued perspectives and mastery in their systems. I learnt a lot about painting, creativity, and process - fulfilling, albeit internally, the central pitch of the series: What can we learn from outside the boundaries of miniature painting.

Here on the page, though, not so much. After talking to everyone the dialectic took over:

  • Thesis: There is so, so much to be learned.
  • Antithesis: I do not have time to learn everything.
  • Synthesis: Here is Joy.

Where I have ended up is perhaps inevitable.

Through intent, structure and finding, this has been a wonderful process, and I have found a great happiness in many stages of it. Contemplating a build not as a task or a hobby but as a compliment to life, a guide to it, a song in the background that swells and breaks (or drops the beat - pay your money and take your choice of genre) when you need it to, has felt so profoundly different to other, hurried, projects that I want to talk about where that joy has been, and to invite you to take nearly eleven months to not even finish a single model. Because, in short, it feels good. Very good.

Joy in the Concept

The concept of the series - and of the Warhound - still, just about, stands. I did learn, mostly about the process of creation from a psychological, philosophical standpoint which perhaps suits me better than technique anyway. The concept of the model though is a real joy. I am no sculptor or artist, I can’t - and never will - do the Jes Goodwin thing (who could? Only the man himself) where a model stands on the page absolutely as it will be in the flesh. I can’t do the Blanche thing (who could? No-one, now) of a drawing that inspires a model where the thread of genius is passed and transmuted between hands until it ends up on the table. What I can do is an idea that I can’t possibly execute, then work joyously within my limits and the materiality of the resin to arrive at an approximation of it. Ultimately, the learning from everyone has been that this process is relational, from start to finish. We engage with material and the world to bring it into ourselves, the object biography that was always there. So I create copy of a copy of a copy, in the way that Celtic coins, when you squint, really do look like a crap version of those of the Macedonian. It’s whisper telephone with myself, a process I have previously found immensely frustrating.

Here, in there, somewhere

Here though I have found joy in it. I have a dim and third hand memory of being mesmerised by a saying tossed out by my grandfather, only to find years later that it was one of the most famous lines of mystic poetry: Your own voice echoing off the walls of God, or, as Google Translate and certainly not my grandfather puts it: Dy lais dy hun yn atseinio o derfynau Duw. There’s no self-aggrandisement here, if my creative process is the walls of god it’s the poorly built, shoddily constructed walls of a crap god (Crap God! The New GrimDark Game from the Makers of….), but letting the concept bounce around as the resin dried in epoxy and sap and what was imagined became what was possible, then what was doable, then just what I was doing in the moment, was a mystical experience. It mutated and flowed, feathers turning from real into wood, then carved, painted and finally merely suggested with angled sponge on metal trim, the body reaching down, the head staring up. The transmutation from Carrion Crow, all sadness and omen, into scrap-hart, renewal and urbanised folkmyth. The failed experiments with bioplastics, and the successful experiments with cyanotype.

A skull changes much

I'd love to say "the most common question I'm asked about working with organic material is their longevity", but no one particularly asks. I've tried to use more organic material than before here - bone, lichen, bark, wool, cotton, wood, mycelium, dyes, shell - and it's come off looking like it usually does. Unusually, though, I've tried to plan for decay. It is already falling apart, the fabrics treated with rusting iron and caustic ashes and crumbling as they are applied, dragging themselves into whisps with the weight of glue and paint pulling fibres apart. The antlers were first mounted with copper rod, then replaced with wood and iron; the monster will shed them, one day, in a cacophonic thunder that shatters everything around it. Feathers, untreated, are fraying and curling. Already, it is different to how it was; once alive, now dying, never dead. Every day it looks different and new. What can we leave behind, what can we rot, what can we let go of? Our models are nigh on infinite, with lives that potentially stretch far, far beyond our own. They are metal and resin and plastic, and we are simply meat. Why not inflict upon them what they inflict upon us?

When I look back at the concept, so little of it remains in substance, but in feeling - those echoes from the walls - it is redolent of it, a beautiful little celebration of my strange, suspended little path. I feel as if it was always there, and all I had to do was chip away at the blessed crow, expel the Bendigiedifran of it all to find what it should have been, amalgam and wild, chaotic refusal of material to behave as it should, already colonised by arachnids and red spider mites (Christ knows what they’re feeding on in there) and wonderfully, solidly present in and of itself. The talking certainly helped that process. Flow, materiality, art, intention, the imagined conversations with mudlarks, the comments, questions, suggestions you’ve given me in various formats, all contributed to switching off the frustration of not being able to pull off exactly what you imagined, to realise that what you create is better - an answer to imagination. An echo. A detail in a wider picture.

Joy in the Detail

There is no cohesive whole here, so that wider picture is just a succession of detail upon detail. There is a broad - very broad - theme of organics, and my paint scheme more or less holds across the titan and the knights that preceded it. But this is a mélange, a mismatch. All detail, or, in another way, all filler no killer. While I enjoy a good unified scheme, I find myself drawn to detail on its own, for the sake of the hour or so spent on each patch. There’s a lot of what I think of as my usual detail here; multilayered rust, chequerboards, the spiraling vines that I’ve been doodling for 30 years in notebooks and essay margins, little birds (and little bits of big ones), leaves, lichen, candles - of course the candles.

Hands, lichen, scribbles

Each section where I’ve added, sculpted, cut, or painted detail is its own project in and of itself, making the Warhound a series of ratty canvases and sketches. I enjoy detail as it suits what I can do these days - half an hour, an hour, stolen time or earned time; the pomodoro method via childcare. As opposed to batch painting or hurrying to get an army done (my goths are languishing as I write this), detail like this completely occupies my focus. Outside of the couple of square inches that expands to occupy all but the most peripheral vision, nothing else exists. There’s both metaphorical and literal elements to that, as hearing drops away and the glasses come off, and as other projects fade into the background. Horizontal lines, vertical lines, fill with black ink, fill with ivory. Breathe, remember to breathe.

Never been a giant fan of oasis

Increasingly I turn to banners and birds, always birds now, the dream of flight filtered through that of Macsen Wledig, as I am torn free of my mid century anchor-ghosts and fall further and further into the past. Kelp takes paint well, inks take the t-shirt scraps, and over time I dress the Warhound in tatters dyed with avocado, nettle, Tumeric, cyanotyping liquid, oak gall and Indian ink.

Dream of Macsen the Bird

Eventually, life breaks through the reverie enough to call me away. An alarm goes off, a child wakes, a lunch break ends, or perhaps the meat calls through one of its many inevitable appetites. The spell breaks, and, hey presto! The detail is done. It’s an approach I’ve been trying to hold on to. Focusing in on an armour panel and deciding it’s done when the time finishes is deeply satisfying. When are models finished? When we say they are. Painting is potentially endless, there will always be something to improve or retouch or redo. But stop! Walk away! It belongs to the ages when your time runs out. Smile and put down the brush, re-enter life renewed. It works, every time.

I've been scribbling this for maybe 30 years

Imagine that process again and again and again. Perhaps a few times a day, or once a week, or, latterly, only when inspiration strikes and a neutrino scything through the matter of the world sparks a neuron in exactly the right way. What is important is the process, and the dance of it, the how of an endless range of potentialities being whittled down into concrete reality. What the detail is - what it looks like, the contribution to the whole, is unimportant. What matters is the movement of my hands across the model, the way that we grip the brush, pin, scalpel or glue, how the pieces are twisted, turned, and affixed. Hands skitter across the workbench for the very fine brush, the neat black, the off white. Too fast, too nervous, we cascade flock, or leaves, or static grass and snow across a blue/white cutting mat, ignored - time to create, but not to improve. It all stays as it is.

Joy in the Accidents

I love that creative impulse in Warhammer that tells us improvement is not necessarily our aim, or even a desirable end. We create! That is enough. It’s a childlike impulse, and I think we lose something in our adulthood with our search for improvement, especially, but not exclusively, with our models. It’s a sense of possibility, I suppose, the imaginative gap that fills better than sprue glue, that turns conversions, those that by any objective sense look like shite, into masterpieces. It’s something that lets everything be joyous. Perhaps you came into this place as an adult - in which case I can only commiserate, because there really is something unique about childhood conversions, no finishing or blending, no additional step: cut, stick.

A child, wanting a model to hold a bigger gun (to shoot better), doesn’t worry about balancing it, or keeping it in proportion, or faction technology, or anything at all, really. They get the bigger gun and they stick it on. Isn’t there a huge and almost forgotten joy in asking What If This Goes There? I remember (hazily, for reasons that will become clear), heating a kitchen knife over the hob until it glowed, so I could cutmelt Space Marine helmets and replace them with skulls - chaos marines straight out of the 2nd edition box set, and cutting all the horse out of Bretonnians to make the first of several dozen mounted wights. Both, of course, look terrible to the eye of adulthood, but I think it’s important to think of these first steps along the way as the start of a journey and the result of one. In and of themselves, they are wonderful, important.

First steps

The horse is something I’d only do without the knowledge of how to do it better. Why is the barding so thick around the eye? Why is it resting on the base? Why did I cut the crest off the helmet and replace it with what I think must be the hair from a tester model of Dark Eldar I got one Games Day long ago? Armed with the knowledge I have now, I wouldn’t do it that way at all - there are many routes to the effect I was after, but carving the living horse out of a box of Bretonnians isn’t one of them. In fact, put those models in my hands again and I’d end up keeping them on the sprue, those vintage ToW guys pay big money for old plastic. Then, I did it regardless, of course, and I played with that phantom Knight army for many, many years. It was impossibly joyous to play it against the conventional armies of my friends and not-so-friendly adults. That was joy, the intersection of teenage diversion and the last shreds of full on childish play.

Behold! The Brain-Breakers. Solar Auxilia, Credit: Lenoon

That’s a place I’ve lost - perhaps you have too - but the Warhound now preens itself in that space, straddling the line between the two on its impossibly weighty base, and gods bless it for that. There is immense satisfaction in all we do here, but it is work. We all find joy in different places - the writing, the painting, the playing, the building, the analysis - but even the most joyous bits sometimes just… aren’t. This is work. Work is hard.

I’d be surprised if it were universal, but I know that some of us - if not many - have at some point hit a burnout with writing, building and painting for review. I know I have, when the sixth Veletaris broke my brain to the extent I gave up Heresy, and however beautiful the models, however lovely the work, you can rapidly alienate yourself from this thing (hobby, site, practice, whatever) that we love. Accidents help with that. You can’t really make mistakes, try out entirely new things or just give it a fucking go when you’re writing for review. You do your painting to your established style, most often because that’s what you know you can pull off quickly. You might try out a technique from one of our HTPEs, but speed and clarity is (usually) the aim of the game.

Not so, of course, here. Instead, I made endless mistakes.

I overcooked the fox femur, making it impossibly brittle. The rawer ends stayed on the Warhound, but the rest was ground into powder and mixed into paint. The paint was scratchy and raw, both aggressive and scared, disobedient and cunning. There’s an animus that drew the warhound more mammalian, that replaced the beak with antlers.

I spilled oak gall ink over the carapace when filling up my fountain pen (which, incidentally, really hates the gall ink), and found it dried to a beautiful translucent sheen, deep in purple and brown tones, as if it were well-loved, ancient wood. Out came the linocutting tools to take best advantage of it, and it ended so beautifully - of all of it, I am most proud of this.

Oak Gall ink, I can't get enough of it

I built the whole torso before remembering I’d intended to fill it full of clockwork to meet and make sense of the treadmill wheel, so now the titan is not powered and moved by manpower, but adorned by servitors attending to a task even more Sisyphean than I’d intended. If we must imagine him happy, I can imagine these miserable, because someone has to be, and it isn’t me - not today.

cut, stick, until the work is done

I tried to carve out the resin of the shoulders smoothly, and royally fucked it, sending a hacksaw spinning into slivers, melting resin via friction of pin and blade, narrowly escaping losing a finger before slamming my hand down (accidentally) on an upturned scalpel blade that earned me 7 stitches. Dried blood makes a thankfully poor primer, so yes, I did wash it off - before anyone asks.  You can fit so much stuff in there, though - wires and gubbins and skulls and birds - and that was joyous, that was the child impulse.

The whole thing, the scaled immensity rocks on its base, a good centimeter of movement at the top. The pins are rigid and well sited, but they’re already working their way through the mdf base. It is precarious, held in place with a sliver of bone under a rear toe that I have not (and will not) paint to match. Measure (never), cut (twice), stick (until it’s full).

Joy in Chasing that High Ever Since

Of course the modelling is to the writing as the heartbeat is to breathing, so there was joy here too. My hobby is here, really, not out there on the board. The writing was, and is, and will be, exultant. That first time I stood twenty feet tall, buoyant on two thousand words lightly edited (knight army, never played). Sometimes my hands burn hot enough to turn iron to vapour sometimes they adhere in frost and for moving them the blood-wreathed bones crack and push through, but however I’m feeling, they can always hit a keyboard at around seventy words a minute. Whatever I’ve written in this process though, the best words came from someone else: make a knight about it.

That's become a mantra, to Make a knight about it. make a knight about it make a knight about it I love it I love it I would make a sticker of it make a t shirt make a banner make a website make a manifesto make a make a make identity about it my thing is that guy who does the weird things makes the toes makes you feel sick makes you feel (mainly tired, and bored, and you roll your eyes) and I love it it is enabling and freeing it is the guy I want to be out in woad and clay with ash dyed hair as an omen of visiting bacchanal but instead I writhe write burn on the bus the 38 the 103 the 4 the SL2 in shirt and jumper but never a tie as if that matters with work shoes on my feet wrapped in the trappings of the weather conscious (always sensibly dressed)

I would like to be the man you read irl, because I love him - and you, thank you for your time. I should get another tattoo.

I step forward with eyes closed, it’s not what I want to do and as fear for my future mounts the model becomes a certainty I can anchor myself around it wobbles on the base with brass rod i can’t remember and I hunt for baize on the streets with the boy I think I am falling apart or coming together I should be able to tell which is which

There is lichen on the floor on fallen bark white birch paper catches my eye and the boy shouts catkin catkin amongst the smoking wreckage the cans and broken glass there is life (comrade ant toils her days away) and there are bones for the pot: One million chickens a day I think, one million avian lives snuffed out to keep the streets coated in bones and the Thames choked with the votive offerings of the last remaining pillars of our nation, the chicken shop, the vape shop. That is the ground I walk on, that is the land my sons and daughter were born into, and this is the place the titan stalks, 28mm scaled with glossy shots in the national psychogeographic.

I am so conscious in this moment of this model as a gift given, and a gift gratefully received. Gifting is many things to many people, isn’t love, but this, this is being seen and understood, enabled, freed, Yes, Yes, Yes, to all my bullshit, to this and to the lack of grammar, and to be given a space to do all this has been a gift, a blessing, i am blessed beyond the ken of mortal and immortal alike, so reach for it and I’ll do the same as we wrench our arms out of sockets to pat each other on the back in this tiny burning moment as the sparrow flies through the window and out again into the darkness. What we leave behind is memory, legacy - and for us, plastic, resin and metal.  When I am gone, what will they do with the Warhound?

Joy in the Repudiation of the False Self

I have taken great, immense, almost painful joy in telling you all these stories over the years. What we’ve spun together has created a new, antagonistic, spikey person, a piece of shit, really, crowing over a hoard of pine and bone. Not the same as, but equally not a million miles from, the author. It has been magical, but I have grown too attached to this particular way of writing and thinking, too self serious, too contrived, too much bullshit, too true (for a given value of truth) so it is time to send him on his journey, and what better time?

I carve a shitty skull out of found bone and bundle it together with rodent bones and broken shards - at this scale not far off a human, albeit a gargantuan, mutated one (but what else are we?). This is a kind of death, a shadow of a requiem for a sliver of a psyche. Aaron has lived, made, written, and now we send him out to sea, coins on his eyes, we watch the coracle buck and turn amidst tossing wave until it falls out of sight. I’m still here - still alive, still writing and building and thinking - but that me isn’t. I make him out of cow, sheep and pig, I dress him in scraps and wrap him in a silken shroud, anointed with lighter fluid and gas. It is kissed and wept over and serenaded.

Then burned on a pyre. Scattered to the winds, to the barrows, on the Warhound, over my keyboard, my brushes. I work it into the cracks of my hands, and smear it across my tools. It is a dark, corrosive dye, a grey and black smear of all that is not but once was. I reek of it, I am indelibly stained with it, by and with all we’ve done together.

title: Overlooked Pokémon cards from Delta Reign are suddenly spiking in price
content:
It's been three weeks since the launch of the latest Pokémon set Delta Reign, and so far its prices show an interesting pattern. While the biggest Delta Reign chase cards (Mega Rayquaza's SIR and gold cards) have seen their price tags fall fairly fast, other hot cards are holding their value, or even increasing their worth.

Rayquaza SIR has fallen from $375 to $285 in just a couple weeks, a precipitous drop that more-or-less follows the pattern for most recent sets. Take Pitch Black and Chaos Rising and their Mega Darkrai and Mega Greninja chases. for instance, to say nothing of 30th Celebration singles.

However, the second place card of the set, Raikou ex, has actually gotten more expensive, moving from $85 to $97 since launch, with a brief spike to $130 last week. It's admittedly fallen somewhat since that quick spike, but seems to be holding steady now.

And it's not the only card to have a kinder price graph than normal. The SIR for Mega Golisopod ex has bounced up in price from $21.30 to $27, while Mega Golurk - though initially falling fast to $25, has since bounced back to $30.

Seeking an explanation for these price changes, I have to agree with YouTuber PTCGRadio. It seems likely that the poor performance of modern Pokémon card singles and sets in recent months led many fans to undervalue these cards. Then, when people realized that Delta Reign had some absolute bangers, the market course-corrected. Of course, the headliner card of the set Rayquaza was already highly hyped up, so its price movements look a lot more normal.

If you're more into your retro cards than modern, you should check out our list of the most expensive rare Pokémon cards of all time. Or come join our Discord server to share your latest pulls!

title: The Tabletop Battles 2026 Gift Guide
content:
Looking for that perfect gift for someone on your list this year, even if that person is you? In our 2026 gift guide, we've got a handful of suggestions to help you make your shopping easier ahead of the big shopping season. In our list you'll find items for most of our core games, as well as some other featured things we just like and think you might like too!

Warhammer 40,000

Warhammer 40,000 Starter Set: USD 255.00

With the release of 11th Edition, now is the perfect time to take the plunge on a Starter Set if you've been considering getting into the game, or know someone who has been. The starter set comes with terrain and a pretty robust set of models to get started with, and when we reviewed it back when it released, we noted that this is one of the most beginner friendly starter kits for newer players.

Warhammer 40,000 Battleforces: USD 255.00 

If you're already established in 40k and looking to expand your army, or want to try a new one, the seasonal Battleforce boxes always make a great option. This year there's sets for Chaos Knights, Necrons, Orcs, Chaos Space Marines, Space Wolves, Space Marines, and Blood Angels, so there's a decent amount of options; if you're really looking to spoil someone (including yourself) a starter set and a Battleforce is a great combo. Campbell goes into more detail on the 40k offerings here!

Age of Sigmar

Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Spearhead Starter Set

Much like with 40k, sometimes one of the best holiday gifts tends to be a starter set, and we think the Spearhead set from 2024 remains one of the best places to start the game from. It is important to note this is not the most recent released set, and we prefer the 2024 set because it makes it very easy to understand the game, get started, and know where to go from here.

Warhammer Age of Sigmar: Battleforces: USD 255.00

And also like 40k, if you know or are someone who already has a pretty solid established set of miniatures and interest in AoS, the Battleforce boxes are always going to do you well. The AoS sets include Knights of Hammerhal, Grunta Stampede, Annihilation Host, Plaugesworn Host, Legion of Damnation, and Court of the Undying King which includes Nagash himself. Campbell has the breakdown of what's what in each box here, if your giftee is a specific fan.

BattleTech

BattleTech Core Box: USD 69.99

If you or someone you know has been Battletech curious for a while now, then the new Core Box from Catalyst is the best possible place to start. It also makes for a pretty affordable gift regardless of the occasion, coming in under 100 USD. If you're on the fence, we reviewed it and think it is one of the best places to start, but also benefits existing players by providing updated materials and models.

Boardgames

Kinfire Delve: USD 20~ and Up

We really enjoyed Kinfire Delve, and it remains a very solid pick for board gaming. If you missed out on it or know a board gamer who might like to give it a shot, the game is very much available and fairly inexpensive compared to other board game offerings on the market at the moment. We also reviewed it, if you'd like to see what Jake had to say about it before hitting buy!

Lord of the Rings: Battle in Balin's Tomb: USD 52.00

I did want to bring attention to the fact that Barnes and Noble lists the game as "Ballin's Tomb", which is very funny, but also, this game is pretty great. It is a Games Workshop product, much like the 40k and Blitz Bowl games you might have seen in Barnes and Nobles before; it may require a little work to find it if you don't have a Barnes and Noble near you, but if you can find it, this is a very solid pick up.

Trench Crusade

Canvas Map: USD 75.00

If you're looking for a gift that's a little off the beaten path of a figure or game piece, this canvas map from Jared Blando of Trench Crusade's world is a really amazing art piece to place up on your gaming or hobby room. there's also a poster variant if you're not that into a canvas map, or if you need to consider budget but still love the illustration.

Trench Crusade: Trench Ghost Bust: USD 70.00

Similarly, Mind Works studios has a pretty impressive collection of busts if you or someone you know is looking for a challenging paint journey. The Trench Ghost bust is an excellent piece that gives a lot of fun options to try bust painting with, and there are a few other Trench Crusade options from the studio (as well as just some general busts that are also pretty cool to consider).

Miscellaneous Gifts

Warhammer Age of Sigmar Gloomspite Gitz Mega Hoodie: USD 99.99

Do I even have to write up why you want one of these? You want one. You know someone else who wants one. You know simply owning this would make your life better, complete, and overall just improved. You can still order it from the GW website, and some stores reportedly still have them, so let me just say that you should run, not walk, to your browser and gift this to yourself and or someone else in your life.

Wr0ng Play! Umamusume Tees: USD 20-33

Do you know an Umamusume fan in your life, or are you one yourself, and you have asked, "I wish that someone would make shirts that go insanely hard and also have them be Umamusume themed"? Well, may I present you with Wr0ng Play's custom tee-shirts that do exactly that. Whether you're getting them as a gag gift, as new fashion statement, or just because they go pretty goddamn hard, the shirts all fit great and are high quality.

Affiliates

As a heads up, the following listings are from our Affiliated partners! If you happen to pick something up from any of them, we do get an amount back, so we wanted to provide this heads up before linking to these partners for the sake of editorial clarity. 

Frontline Gaming

We're big fans of Frontline Gaming's terrain and mats, and we use them at our own events and at home. If you're looking for something to help build up your gaming space or table and you've already got all of the models you could ever need, investing in a solid gaming mat is a great way to ensure that your models, dice, and terrain all last a lot longer, as well as just improving the overall look of your table.

The Army Painter

There are a lot of painting options on the market right now, and that makes it kind of complicated to suggest any specific set, product, or type of paint; you probably know what works best for you, or the person you're shopping for, but if you're looking for something that can make shopping easy for the beginner hobbyist to the expert, Army Painter is a solid choice for many options and skill levels.

Elegoo

While this isn't exactly an endorsement of 3D printing or suggesting that 3D printing is for you, we've worked with and reviewed the Elegoo products for a while now, and stand by that they are a quality product that we don't mind being affiliated with. If anything, these are one of the bigger investments on the list, so absolutely make sure this is something you, or your giftee, wants and needs!

Victrix

If you or your giftee are into Historicals, then our partnership with Victrix is perhaps one of the best options for a wide variety of Historical miniatures, and also for picking up the ruleset for Pillage, which we really pretty high on. Their range includes medieval, Napoleonic, WW2, and more, and Victrix has long been one of the most reliable names in 28mm wargaming.

Bandua

Finally, we are pretty happy with the terrain offerings from Bandua, and if you're looking for terrain for your table, consider whether or not Bandua is right for you. We also quite like their carrying cases, and frankly have always been happy with the products we've reviewed and received from them; again if you're looking for something other than just miniatures or rulesets, Bandua has a lot of options for a lot of various gaming systems.

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Rakshasa
content:
Ella Entrali eased back in her command couch, her eyes wandering over the distant rolling plains to the east of Plymouth Landing. They were out there somewhere, she had thought, scurrying like rats amongst the dense copses of tellen oaks. It was her against the world out here, or at least her against the coming medium lance the Curiassier overflight had given her a tip on.

She liked Pirates about as much as the next Marshal, she supposed, there was little love lost amongst the ranks of her new compatriots for the raiding scoundrels that tried to prey on the Reaches’ populace. Though her grudge drove deeper than theirs. Theirs was a culture, it seemed, instilled and hammered into the people of the Periphery, even those who’d never met a Pirate or even seen a raid land on their continent, let alone their world, in a generation. 

Hers was personal. 

Gloved fingers slid across the arms of her aging Rakshasa’s command couch, tracing the Davion Sun and Shield emblem that hadn’t quite been worn away by her worrying yet. She’d always swore she’d get it replaced when she left, dropped her contracts to seek somewhere that at least felt like it cared, but she could never bring herself to do it. Despite her current life she was still a Davion girl at heart, had bit the lines of Liberty, Freedom, and Justice hook, line, and sinker like no one else in her command when she was in the Syrtis Fusiliers. 

Gung-ho as could be and ready to take the fight to whatever the First Prince pointed her and hers at. Annoying enough about it to get ‘Patriot’ as a callsign even. Then when it mattered the call never came.

She still has nightmares about the holo-vids of Travis burning to the ground, watching helplessly as her home turned to ash and the call to defend them never came. The call for retribution never came. The call to do something… never came.

Her hand slipped from the couch, fishing an old family locket out from the depths of her cooling suit before thumbing it open with a soft click that blended in with the hum and bustle of the cockpits machinery. It was an old picture from before she was born, her ma and pa sat on their porch at home on the outskirts of Travis. A porch that she’d imagined a Firestarter putting to the torch a million times while just a jump away.

Tears welled behind her eyes, threatening to spill forth as she stared at the heirloom, mumbling a prayer to whoever counted as listening in the great void of the sphere that there was something better in death than had met them in life. 

And that she get a chance to keep someone else from feeling her own pain. 

Copy Cat’s sensors chirped, stealing her from her ever-spiraling thoughts as she looked up from the pendant and out at the gathering dust cloud billowing skyward to her north. Four contacts, a pair of old ramshackle medium mechs, a Firestarter, and an ancient succession wars Grasshopper.

She tracked them for a moment, watching as they ducked and bobbed amongst the trees, cutting a beeline for the Plymouth’s northern port warehouses. Copy Cat rumbled and hummed as she spurred it up and onwards, whispering silent thanks into the cockpit before drawing her guns down on the Firestarter as it broke left towards an outlying warehouse. She squeezed the firing studs as the sight settled on the lead track and the MMLs screamed tone for an LRM solution. 

The particle beams lanced out, spearing the little light ‘Mech in its right shoulder, the force carrying the arm away with it as the AMS on its left tried and failed to intercept the falling missiles. She grinned as the machine stumbled and fell on its side, reaching up to key her radio as she drove her Rakshasa to its full speed. “Curiassiers, four ‘Mech contacts north of Plymouth in Saloon quadrant. Mark Marshals as engaging.”

Time to get some retribution.

– Marshal Ella Entrali, Fronc Reaches, Colonial Marshal Rakshasa MDG-1Ar Pilot. Spencer, Fronc Reaches, February 23rd 3105. 

Howdy Mechwarriors and welcome back to another Mech Overview! Yes yes, I know, we already technically covered the Rakshasa before… but see that was then and this is now, and now we’ve got an actual model for it! A damn good looking model at that!

And a new variant! Yippee!

So, what is a Rakshasa? Well, simply put, it’s an IS attempt to capture the glory and splendor of a MAD CAT without using Clan Tech or making it an Omni-Mech. This was my friend over at GM’s new-designs division’s first attempt to chase glory in that realm and they, largely, did a pretty alright job at it! They cranked out a 75 ton heavy ‘Mech that apes the basic Prime config of the Mad Cat and did the best they could with what they had. My Clan advisor has advised me that this is indeed a ‘lowly spheroid imitation not worth our time or attention over the glory that is the Timber Wolf’. Well, IDK about her but I love the Rakshasa so I decided that, with the new core box hitting shelves, it’d be a great time to go back over it…

No other reason. Definitely nothing to do with the core box’s ‘Mech cards having a Colonial Marshals Rakshasa, or that art also appearing in the Core Box rule book, or in the general Core rulebook either… That’s absurd, that’s definitely not why I’m doing this. Anyhow, look at this pretty bitchin’ Rakshasa I painted!

Marshal Ella 'Patriot' Entralli's Rakshasa 1Ar 'Copy Cat', Credit: Liberty

Chassis

The Rakshasa, despite not being an Omni-Mech is very Omni-like. Every variant moves 5/8, has an IS XL engine, and a pretty good clip of ammo occupying the side torso. Additionally they all share the exact same armor load, except the MDG-1Ar which adds 1 pip to the CT Front and Rear, it goes like this:

  • 21 on the arms
  • 22 on the side torsos
  • 32 on the CT front
  • 28 on the legs
  • 7/9/7 across the rear.

This is an 89% coverage rate, or 206 pips, which is a touch thin but still thick enough all over to be quite functional for a cavalry heavy that usually wants to be skirmishing at you from the edge of its short range to hopefully keep the damage off its back. If you end up in a position where an AC/20 is after you then at least you can stay safe in the knowledge that it is going to have to get some other guns on you to manage to go in anywhere!

Also, they all have 15 double heat sinks?

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘Mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology). Our reviews focus on using these mechs in an 8-10k BV game playing the Core Rules missions. 

MDG-1A

RUN, IT’S A MAD CA- Oh, no, nevermind, just a Rakshasa.

The MDG-1A is the original copy. The best of the bootlegs you’ll find on the street corner GM lot. It does what it says on the tin, just a bit worse. Aping the Mad Cat Prime configs loadout we’ve got a pair of IS ER Large Lasers and a pair of Medium Lasers out in the arms, a Medium Pulse laser in the left torso, and a pair of LRM 10 racks up on the shoulders with Artemis IV for a nice little damage boost. The LRM bins are a bit smaller than the PTSD delivery device that its chasing but the Rakshasa’s doing the best that it can with the tonnage spread that its got.

This is, honestly, a fine enough loadout even without being Clan Tech. Where a Mad Cat Prime would cost 2,737 The MDG-1A costs a far more reasonable, and workable, 1,795 BV that is far easier to slip into a list like it’s wearing nothing at all.

Heat wise it’s quite manageable in here, with 15 double heat sinks you’ve got the heat management to sling both ERLLs and one of the LRM bins on the run while heat neutral or you can build movement heat to close in and sling the arm guns. The MPL is kinda just hanging on for dear life here but that’s fine, it’s for when you decide you’re ok bumping the heat scale a little bit to tell a fire moth it’s not welcome here.

Just be careful, that’s enough firepower to make said fire moth blink out of existence entirely. Do you really want that on your conscience?

Liberty’s Rating: C+. She’s no world beater but she’s a damned fine enough ‘Mech, and damned fine enough ‘Mechs get damned fine enough ratings.

Dawn Guard Rakshasa. Credit: Jack Hunter

MDG-1Ar

Refit Time? God I love Refit Time. It’s always fuckin’ dumb.

Oh, oh this isn’t dumb at all.

This is, unequivocally, my favorite of the Rakshasas. If I have a Rakshasa on a table it’s probably this one. Equipped with two of my favorite guns the 1Ar has a pair of Snub-nosed PPCs and a pair of MML 7s with 3 tons of ammunition in a CASE protected bay. Also there are some medium lasers here.

You’ve got the sinking to dump both snubs and both MML 7s into something and be heat neutral on the run, or up movement if you fire off the snubs, the mediums, and one MML 7. Of note this is enough ammo to play quite a quite fun game with specialty ammo types! At standard it comes with 2 tons of LRM and 1 ton of SRM. I, personally, take it with 1 LRM, 1 SRM Standard, and 1 SRM Inferno for pressing advantages, or disadvantages, when I find them.

For 1,675 BV I adore this thing. I have bothered, badgered, bugged, begged, and bedeviled the Force Marshal to get them to buy a company of 1As and the refit kits so that we might assemble what is undoubtedly one of the most Marshal coded Heavy ‘Mechs in the sphere.

God I want this fucking thing on the Fronc Avail more than anything else.

Liberty’s Rating: A-. This is an incredibly efficient device, capable of significant range band play and close in punishment when someone’s getting thin on the armored tooth while having enough of a belt on it to weather the punishment it takes in return. I love this damned thing to the moon and back and it truly is a prized child of mine.

MDG-1B

Wait a second… I’ve seen this one before.

This is a 1A but with the ERLLs turned into LLs. That’s it, that’s the change. This at least makes it so you can fire all the energy guns off at once with one of the LRM bins and only build movement heat?

Close in this has some slightly better damage potential over the 1A since it can bring more little lasers to bear, but IDK that I’d call it worth 1,748 BV. Yea, this is only 47 BV cheaper than the 1A and it appears on all the same avails. I mean, I’ll take it, I guess?

Liberty’s Rating: C+. I think with the speed of the Rakshasa I can jive with this, an option to run in close and turn on the light show isn’t a bad thing, just wish it was a touch cheaper since it’s dropping a fair bit of closing/snapshot capabilities.

Battletech Rakshasa triumphant over those Fakers. Credit: Perigrin.

MDG-2A

DO YOU HEAR IT? THE CHATTERING HOWL OF GNASHING GEARS AND DRIVING MOTORS? DO YOU HEAR THE SOUNDS OF THE AMMO CLATTERING AND CLANKING INTO THE BREACH? I DO, I HEAR THE CALL OF THE WORLD’S ENGINE AND I RELISH IN ITS BARKING REPORT AND SEARING PULSES! I AM THE GUN-CAT, AND YOU SHALL ALL FEAR MY NAME!!!

The 2A is the first Rakshasa to fully depart from the vague shape of the OG Mad Cat Prime, fully doing its own thing! So, what is the Rakshasa’s ‘own thing’?

Simple:

  • A Large Pulse Laser in the right arm
  • 4 Medium Pulse Lasers, 2 in the right arm 2 in the right torso
  • A Rotary AC/5 in the left arm
  • 3 tons of Rotary AC/5 ammunition in the left torso

This is 1,766 BV for a moving mass of hate and firepower that wants to sprint at something and spin up the gun to full tilt and let it rip its vast anger into whatever has the poor sense to stand there and take it. At full tilt you build 2+movement which means on the run you drop an MPL and let the rest of it eat.

Go forth, Davion ‘Mechwarrior, and let slip the Cats of War.

Liberty’s Rating: B+. If not for the 1Ar this would be my favorite Rakshasa and its not close. I’ve used it a few times to pair with the 1Ar in the GMGM and it does an astounding job when supported right.

Rakshasa painted by Raymond Cracker, image provided by Catalyst Game Labs

MDG-3D

Clan Guns? In my Clan imposter? More likely than you think!

The 3D is the new Core Box variant! It’s… man it’s something. Going back to the path of aping the Mad Cat Prime’s config we’ve got a pair of cERLLs and cERSLs out in the arms, a cERML in the left torso, and a pair of… oh, great. I was wondering what fun new things we might get out of the tonnage saved on the better guns and was really hoping the answer would be a T-Comp with some cLRMs or maybe some more heat sinks…

It’s not that. It’s a pair of Extended LRM 10s with one ton of ammo each. Hell, they didn’t even bother to put the ammo in a CASE protected bay.

This is 2,100 BV.

It’s got use cases, if you’re gonna do some big ol’ BFM sized games this could certainly get some work done but in a normal close in game those ELRMs may as well not exist. So, what's the laser heat look like? It can rip the ERLLs and ERSLs off and be heat neutral on the run. This kinda just means that the cERML is like… there? 2100 BV for 30 consistent damage output is uh, not great. Not great at all.

Liberty’s Rating: D. Why must you do things like this, Rakshasa? Why must you hurt me so when you had such awesome potential? Trade those ELRMs for some LRMs with Artemis V and a T-Comp and I’d think this was fucking awesome. You can make it fit, I checked.

Final Thoughts

I really do love the Rakshasa. I’ve loved it since I first looked at it, hell a change to the 1Ar to futz with the ammo and secondaries was one of the first customs I ever made! It has good movement, good armor, acceptable guns, and great prices for what it does!

We stan the Rakshasa in this house, and I will broker no insults upon her name. Anyone who does can meet me in the periphery version of a circle of equals, the back lot of the local Waffle House.

Try me.

Until next time! Fair weather, good seas and happy infuriating-the-weird-furries-from-the-deep-periphery-ing!

title: [40K] Competitive Innovations in 11th: Hark, Angels pt.1
content:
Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our weekly feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Each week our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the week’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

The World Championships looms ever closer, and right now Space Marines look poised to claim it. All of Iron Hands, Ultrawatch, Dark Angels and Space Wolves are tearing up the metagame, and although there's still sparks of defiance, this week they're firmly on top. Will the tables turn once the best of the best unleash their super secret tech? Not long till we find out. For now, let's survey the power-armoued devastation.

Advance Warning - Next Week's Column

It is reasonably likely that this column will be disrupted next week, as both your regular columnists (and most of the people we'd normally trick into covering for us) are at the World Championships of Warhammer. We'll do our best, but there may be some scheduling changes!

Thoughts

We start as we mean to go on today with some Dark Angels representation, here repping a big pile of Speeders with bonus alpha strike potential via Thundercowl Turbines. Nasty. The army shoots real good, and has a powerful roving melee threat from Sammael and co, and that's kind of all you need. The one novelty to highlight is running an Impulsor with the option on heavy bolter Eradicators instead of melta. The list already has a tonne of anti-tank, so packing in some insurance against things like 20-Berzerker bricks seems fine, sure. Dark Angels wildly outperformed everyone else on win rate this weekend, even if I think the most powerful Wolves and Iron Hands builds are probably better, but even amongst all these successes this was the single biggest win, so congratulations Jack!

As this has been happening we've seen lists without as many Dreadnoughts do well, but you absolutely can still just slam Dreadnoughts and Allarus onto the table and go wild. This combination of tools gives you a great ability to push into pretty much all Marine builds, though dropping the Caladius that you normally see reduces threat projection against some forces. Teching for the Marine matchup makes sense though - emerging evidence is that the Custodes book is extremely real, but because of its low drop count it suffers into enemies that are just too efficient, which the best Marines absolutely are. This build feels right for that metagame, and though it couldn't quite pin down the Dark Angels above, it did smash through several other powerful Marine lists with Steve at the helm.

Thoughts

The Imperium's most elite forces face off, presumably arguing over who gets to fumigate the basement of the Imperial Palace for the next century. In the shiny silver corner, a Purifier-heavy build of Warpbane, going for a second full squad as well as Crowe's, which is currently the most popular option for Warpbane. This is because when storm bolters are real guns, it turns out that being able to fire a whole squad of them with full hit and wound re-rolls is pretty good in most matchups.

Not so much this one though - this has the potential to be fairly rough. The good-ish news for the Grey Knights is that Custodes don't have the drops to screen out their teleporting nonsense, especially if they prioritise clearing the Sisters, so they can leverage mobility very effectively. They're also well set up to take the Terminators off the board if given a chance, though Trajann's sheer durability may well bounce them.

The bad news is the rest of this army, which is very resilient to their offence, and perfectly equipped to send them back to Titan. Double Caladius is a disaster for the Grey Knights - unless they get turbo-lucky with the razorbacks, these are never dying, and threaten to obliterate a Dreadknight cleanly each time they shoot. Meanwhile, the Galatus dreads are fantastic into everything that they're facing, and hard to put down. The Custodes being Emperor's Chosen is especially bad for the Grey Knights, as they're very reliant on big swings with AP-1 and AP-2 weaponry, which In Auramite Clad can blunt. Given that the mission combination also forces the Grey Knights to take the initiative, this feels like it goes very badly unless the Custodes screw up or get disastrously unlucky. As the Knights, your best chance to make that happen is to clear the Sisters as a priority, then try to exploit the freedom to warp around the table, but it's going to be super uphill, and so it proved here.

Thoughts

The latest addition to the collection of Space Marine horrors rounds out the undefeated podium here, bringing to bear a level of firepower and tricks more normally seen in release-strength Aeldari books, attached to the durability of Marines. This won't be the last we'll see of this army this week, as (spoilers) Innes also took it to a top finish, and let me tell you by the time I'd listened to all the wild things it could do, I wasn't happy. Elsewhere, lots of the army can pull the "exciting" trick of Overwatching then moving d6", i.e. Phantasm but with firepower, and this is especially upsetting on the Invictors, who have a massive number of shots and are deadly into hordes in particular thanks to their flamers. I am already mentally preparing myself for pairing into this in round 1 of the WCW. I don't think we'd need the four-hour round time. Congratulations Ian.

Reaper's Wager flips into fourth place here, combining all the best Drukhari herohammer with a large, Ingress Troupe. As the title suggests, this is the build of Shamblerot that excelled at the Paris Wargame Expo a little while ago, dropping the standard Defiler and also using the flex slot for Plague Marines and Plaguecasters in Rhinos. This gives the list a more mid-weight piece it can skirmish with compared to the polarised Poxwalker or Engine options you normally have, and also makes locking down objectives and reliably hitting Disruption Primary much easier. The Knight still gives you plenty of long-ranged firepower, which is helped by the Plague Marines being able to tag bonus AP onto a more distant target. This version also loses a lot less from the change to Shambling Wall than Defiler versions, and it wouldn't shock me if we saw it creep further up in popularity. Fundamentally, the Plague Marine datasheet is an absolute steal at 90pts, so congratulations to Marc for putting them to work.

title: This Fuchöv castle is the coolest Warhammer terrain I've seen in years
content:
Some people get into Warhammer for the story, others chase the thrill of competition, and others take joy in painting. Me? I'm in it for the dollhouses. My terrain obsession probably stems back to the double whammy of Necromunda and then Mordheim in the late 1990's, which taught me that miniatures never look cooler than when they're fighting over a ruined building. And if you share my obsession, you should check out Fuchöv castle by TerraBloks, which is… well, the name says it all.

Fuchöv castle is a 3D printable digital scenery set. If you've got an FDM printer and enough filament, it contains enough files for you to print a complete, terrain-packed, 6′ by 8′ foot gaming table. Two tables, in fact, because the set comes with both an intact and a ruined version of the castle.

Assuming you print this "out of the box", you'll have a massive and cinematic table divided between two rocky islands, connected by a bridge. One of them is relatively open except for a gatehouse, while the other is taken up with the castle itself. Particularly in its ruined state, this gives me FromSoftware vibes - it reminds me of both the keeps from Elden Ring and the Painted World of Ariamis from the original Dark Souls.

The Kickstarter campaign for Fuchöv castle is over but it's still accepting pledges. A set with the ruined and intact versions of the castle, the risers, scatter terrain stretch goals, and connection blocks to integrate with previous sets, will set you back $94 (£72). And if you want to test out the quality of the terrain, you can download a free windmill set from MyMinifactory.

I could pick holes in the architecture of the ruined version of the castle; there are a lot of floors and partially demolished walls suspended over thin air with no obvious supports. But it's clear that the creator, Andy Green, designed this with gaming in mind. It looks like you'll have decent access to your models wherever they are on the board, and the stairs are even designed so models can stay put on them without sticky tack thanks to regular landings or gaps you can wedge bases in.

While many of the buildings in the default build are interconnected, the set comes with variants designed to be printed as standalone terrain. The rocky risers aren't just for looks, they raise the ground level to match TerraBloks' existing 'Helwick' terrain system, which has playable basements beneath all the buildings - but you can ditch the risers and keep just the top layer of the rocky island and use that as the board in itself.

TerraBloks says its models can be printed on regular FDM printers without any supports; I haven't tested the claim (I'm currently making a mixture of Factory Fortress and HexBrick terrain for a Trench Crusade board…). If you've printed off some TerraBloks kits, or can recommend any other great sources of Warhammer terrain, share some pictures in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: From the archives: Fallout: the Roleplaying Game is a love letter to the Bethesda RPGs
content:
This article was originally published on November 9, 2021.

Fallout: The Roleplaying Game, the officially licensed tabletop RPG 'port' of Bethesda Softworks' post-apocalyptic open world videogame series, has to be the most visually on-brand TTRPG adaptation I've come across. Fallout's distinctive, tragi-comic 'Vault Boy' cartoon artworks, pastel-colored retrofuturist adverts and propaganda, and the ubiquitous blue-and-gold livery of Vault-Tec all saturate the rulebook's 430 tight-packed, glossy pages. Even merely as hardback eye-candy, its looks are worth the asking price.

Don't be fooled , however - this is no superficial, low-effort, licensed cash-in. Publisher Modiphius has form for doing justice to beloved fictional worlds while translating them to the world of dice and pencils, having already used its rather well-received 2D20 rules system to make tabletop roleplaying games out of Star Trek, and, more recently, Dune. Serious legwork went into producing this game; that much is clear from the sheer number of the videogames' mechanics, characters, concepts, and items that get their own developed tabletop rules.

I've so far had only a few snatched, glorious hours to trawl through Fallout: The Roleplaying Game's core book (let alone actually play the damn thing) so by all means take this particular can of Pork 'n' Beans with a pinch of salt.

But even a cursory tour around this tabletop RPG left me with one overwhelming impression: that it is, first and foremost, a laudably comprehensive attempt to translate every single aspect of the more recent Bethesda videogames into tabletop form (the more nostalgic and warmly remembered by gamers, the better).

When we reported on the game's crowdfunding launch earlier in 2021, we got rather excited about the fact that Fallout: The Roleplaying Game lets you play as a Mister Handy robot, Super Mutant, or Ghoul - but that's honestly just the tip of the iceberg here. Let's take a brief tour.

Action Points, Perks, and Dogs, oh my!

Modiphius' 2D20 game system has two big selling points: first, the flexibility with which it allows GMs to mix and match characters' attributes and skills to apply to specific tests; and, second, its potential for 'push your luck' gameplay, with superfluous successful rolls able to be banked and spent to boost other tests, or for assorted benefits.

Fallout: The Roleplaying Game makes neat use of the former aspect; characters' attributes (naturally) follow the videogames' S.P.E.C.I.A.L. system, while the game's list of Skills comes straight out of Fallout 3 - with the new additions of Athletics, Throwing, and Pilot (because you never did let me fly a Vertibird on my Xbox 360, Bethesda, you cowards).

As for pushing one's luck with stored boosts to tests, well, if you thought "that sure sounds like spending Action Points to use V.A.T.S. to kill things better" - then you're right on Modiphius' wavelength. Roll more successes than needed for a test, and you can bank each unneeded die as one Action Point - then cash 'em in later to roll extra dice on another test, take extra actions on your turn, get info from the GM, or any of various other boons.

Want even more ways to swing your rolls and tell stories with dice? Lucky you. In the videogames, the Luck (LCK) attribute makes multiple, behind-the-scenes tweaks to gameplay calculations - but, in Fallout: The Roleplaying Game, Luck gets a bit more 'hands on'.

You start each quest with a pool of Luck Points equal to your LCK stat, and can spend them to re-roll dice; interrupt the initiative order in combat; substitute your Luck stat for another attribute when rolling a test; or even make subtle, but helpful changes to the scene around you. It's a limited system, but could go some way to recreating the sense of being a powerful protagonist that suffuses the videogame experience.

Also just like the videogames, as you level up, you'll pick Perks that add buffs (and sometimes drawbacks) to your character, and start to shape your character's particular profile. All your familiar favorites are back - Bloody Mess; Sniper; Lead Belly; Black Widow; Lady Killer; even the ever-entertaining Mysterious Stranger can be called upon to aid you in a fight (with a particularly beasty, stat-boosted .44 Magnum).

And guess what else pops up as a Perk? It's only bloody Dogmeat, everyone's favorite wasteland canine pal, complete with his own tabletop RPG stat block, and - get this - craftable dog armor. There is an entire separate armor crafting table for dog armor. It doesn't even cost extra as DLC (only joking Todd, jeez). And, while we're on the subject of tables…

Tables for days

This book contains a stupendous library of stats tables for items and effects that'll be familiar to anyone who's played Fallout 3, New Vegas, or Fallout 4.

There are 27 pages of weapons; six pages of normal armor; five types of Power Armor chassis with a variety of pieces and upgrades for each; seven pages full of chems; and a whopping 15 pages of wasteland food and drink items. On top of that, every weapon and armor piece can take a variety of craftable upgrade mods, each of which are listed in their own respective tables.

The extensive, 18-page crafting system includes stats tables for reams of armor pieces, weapons, mods, chems, and food recipes that you and your party can throw together (if you've got the right Workbench, Cooking Station, and/or crafting ingredients). It's positively breathtaking how much the rulebook reads like the numerical backend to Fallout 4 itself.

As for the rad-twisted beasts of post-nuclear America, their particulars are listed out to a T in a chunky 60-page bestiary, from Bloodbugs to Yao Guai, and Super Mutants to Synths. Gorgeous (and often gruesome) artworks abound, as do GM notes, alternate creature versions, and copious, clearly laid out special abilities.

And that's before we've even mentioned the stacks of narrative background to the Commonwealth wasteland setting of Fallout 4; the entire chapters on pre-war corporations and Vault-Tec vaults; or the fully-fledged three-act starter adventure provided right in the core rulebook. This book might be a weighty tome with much to wrap one's irradiated head around - but it makes an effort to give you ways in.

Heavy duty doomsday

All of which makes Fallout: The Roleplaying Game less like an indirect homage to the Bethesda Fallout videogame experience - and more like an ambitious and rather spectacular bid to recreate it all for you, wholesale - insanely detailed sandbox and all. Modiphius isn't trying to make a tabletop RPG, set in the Fallout universe; it's trying to let you actually play Fallout 4, only without using a computer.

Which could be fantastic, or an absolute dead loss - depending, I suppose, on what sort of Fallout fan you are. Whichever way you cut it, though, it's one hell of an elevator pitch. Personally, I can't wait to give it a proper run for its money - I'm just waiting till I've saved up enough caps for the cool custom dice…

Want to hear more about the best tabletop RPGs in the biz? Check out our cultivated guide, or ask for some recs in the Wargamer Discord.

title: MTG sues alleged counterfeiter laundering money through sticker websites
content:
Wizards of the Coast is suing a popular proxy company which it claims is using sticker companies to launder money made through Magic: The Gathering copyright infringement. It argues that PrintMTG is producing counterfeit MTG cards through multiple websites and using the label of 'proxy' as a fig leaf. The complaint, filed with the US District Court on November 23, accused PrintMTG's owners of "trademark infringement, counterfeiting, and criminal copyright infringement on a grand scale".

So what's the difference between proxying and counterfeiting? That's key to this lawsuit, as WotC believes PrintMTG is passing one off as the other. According to Wizards, "An honest proxy is a stand-in for a real card that makes no claim to authenticity, by appearance or otherwise." Meanwhile "a counterfeit is made to be mistaken for the real card".

Which activity is PrintMTG engaged in? Well, despite PrintMTG's websites disavowing fakes - "that's not what we're here for" says one - WotC alleges that its unlicensed use of real Magic artwork, trademarks, frames, and backs make it a counterfeiter. It points to its advertising describing the cards' authentic, realistic, and professional feel. One of the websites, ProxyKing, states that their cards "let you join games and play without people noticing you are running proxy cards in your Magic deck."

The rest of the document reveals that Wizards has engaged in (or more likely paid someone else to do) some serious detective work. It lays out more of PrintMTG's alleged wrongdoings, describing an intricate web of false aliases and shell corporations that were apparently used by the owners, identified as Utah residents, to cover their tracks.

It claims the defendants created multiple sticker-selling websites like YouStickers.com and CustomStickers.com "as a front through which to launder the revenue gained from their widespread infringement of Wizards' intellectual property". It accuses them of taking pains to present these as competing businesses, with fake names and backstories, to inflate the apparent size of the sticker trade.

It also alleges "the PrintMTG Enterprise maintains dozens of websites which purport to review YouStickers and CustomStickers against each other or against third-party sites, almost always ranking CustomStickers at #1 and YouStickers at #2." Again, these are said to be owed by people that do not truly exist, and the conflict of interest is never stated.

As well as fake Magic cards, the enterprise also allegedly traded in fake Pokémon cards and Lego minifigures, but Wizards of the Coast is understandably less directly concerned about these. For its various complaints, the company is seeking $28 million in damages.

Wargamer has reached out to PrintMTG Enterprise for comment.

The whole story makes for an interesting read. I'm expecting to see a RecklessBen video about it any time now. If you've got a hot take, I'd love to hear it over on the Wargamer Discord.
