There are a very few shadowless cards that aren't first edition, but it's the combination of the shadowless border and first edition logo that's the real certification of excellence.

In October 2020, a PSA 10 mint condition first-edition shadowless holographic Charizard was bought by ex-rapper Logic at auction for a sizeable $220,000 (£173,000), only to be surpassed a month later when another Charizard of the same specifications sold for $295,000 (£210,000).

A mint PSA 10 copy sold in 2022 for $420,000 (£334,000) via Fanatic Collect (formerly PWCC Marketplace) - but in April 2026, Collectr reported a private sale from Benjamin Be to Thiago Nigro for $700,000. That makes the First edition Charizard, once again, the most expensive playable Pokémon card in the world.

4. Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer

Price$1,769,000
Sale dateMay 18, 2026
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

It might feel odd for the third prize Trophy Pikachu card from the Pokémon TCG's earliest Japanese tournaments to sell for four times as much as the second prize card did in 2023. That's especially true, given both cards had the same perfect PSA 10 grading, both have a similar, vanishingly small population of PSA graded cards, and both were the only PSA 10 copy known to be in existence at the time of sale.

But that's exactly what happened: in May 2026, New Jersey auctioneers Goldin (yes, the ones from TV) sold the single confirmed Trophy Pikachu No.3 Trainer for a winning bid of $1.45 million - totalling 1,769,000 bucks after a 22% buyer premium. Why the huge price difference? Maybe the buyer liked the adorably tiny trophy; maybe the bronze sparkly finish simply looks a bit more like the gold of the No. 1 trophy card below.

Or maybe, in between 2023 and 2026, Pokémon cards have begun attracting so much more attention from the ultra-wealthy that the very rarest specimens are now a fashionable status symbol for billionaires (or those who wish to appear to be billionaires) to flaunt at each other.

Maybe the top end of this is mostly an ego playground for fabulously rich men who'll happily spend $1.77m - the cost of 4.1 million meals for starving people, according to the World Food Programme - on a 2.5 by 3.5 inch rectangle of cardboard, just because they can. Does it bring them as much joy as it brought a Japanese teenager at the end of one triumphant weekend in the late 90s? We can only imagine.

3. Trophy Pikachu No. 1 Trainer

Price$3,000,000
Sale dateSeptember 12, 2025
Auction houseeBay
GraderPSA
RatingMINT 9

Sitting right at the top of the Trophy Pikachu Tree, fittingly, is 1998's Trophy Pikachu No.1 Trainer - extremely limited promos handed only to the winning Pokémon players at the TCG's second-ever sanctioned tournament, the 1997-98 Japanese Lizardon Mega Battle Pokémon competition.

Just like its promo prize siblings, the number-one Pikachu was illustrated by Mitsuhiro Arita. This time, the world's most popular Pokémon is lifting a trophy in the air, grinning in triumph.

Supposedly, there are only 14 copies of this card, period. We've seen others sell for thousands upon thousands, but none have quite matched the price of the copy sold in September 2025. It's understandable - MINT 9 might be the best grading we've ever seen this promo get. No.1 Trainer Pikachu is a true winner, indeed.

2. Raincoat Pikachu - perhaps

Price$8,400,000
Sale dateSeptember 28, 2026
Auction houseFanatics Collect
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

Raincoat Pikachu was created as a prize for a competition tied to the 3DS game Pokémon Art Academy in 2015; fans had to draw Pikachu in the game and upload it to the Miiverse social network. Six winners each got 100 copies of the promotional Pikachu card featuring their very own illustration.

This is a rare card to be sure, and in September 2026 a copy sold for a massive $8,400,000 (including buyer's premium) on Fanatics Collect - at least, it seems like it did. There's actually some doubt.

Reporters at Chase Society noticed that this auction listing was removed from Fanatics Collect entirely, which is usually a sign that the buyer has failed to pay. The listing then returned to the site. As of November 13 2026 it's still up, but scrutinizing the page source data shows that it has the "cancelled" status. There's an error in the data, it's just not clear where, so we're keeping an eye on this one.

1. Pikachu Illustrator

Price$16,492,000
Sale dateFebruary 16, 2026
Auction houseGoldin
GraderPSA
RatingGEM MT 10

The new holy grail of the TCG, Pikachu Illustrator is a promo Pokémon card originally handed out to winners of a 1998 illustration competition run through Japanese magazine CoroCoro. Only 39 copies were ever created.

It's the only card to feature the 'Illustrator' title instead of 'Trainer'. The artwork was drawn by esteemed Pokémon illustrator Atsuko Nishida, creator of Pokémon's main mascot, Pikachu. There's even a unique pen icon in the bottom-right corner, seen on no other card.

It's unknown exactly how many Pikachu Illustrator cards are still in existence, but ten PSA certified copies have been graded as 'mint'. From January 2021 onwards, it was the most expensive Pokémon card to ever be sold at auction, with a PSA 9 Mint condition card selling for a whopping $233,000 (£167,600).

Though it lost the title briefly, in July 2021 Logan Paul (yeah, that guy) spent $4 million on the only existing PSA 10 version of the card, getting the purchase accredited by Guinness World Records as the most expensive Pokémon card ever sold. But the value of the card was actually even higher: to secure the trade, Paul also handed over a lesser PSA 9 version of the card, which he'd previously purchased for $1,275,000.

The saga of this card doesn't end there. In early 2026, Mr Paul went on to sell the card to one AJ Scaramucci, once again getting Guinness involved. That's because the sales figure this time was a frankly staggering $16,492,000.

We should add that Logan also parted ways with the diamond-encrusted necklace he'd been carrying the card around in (does a $1 card taped to a $2 million car cost $2,000,001?) But even so, it's more than fair to call this the most expensive Pokémon card of all time!

It's a pity it's so rare: Pikachu looks even cuter than usual holding an oversized fountain pen.

Bonus - Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack

Price$2,700
Sale dateUnverified
Auction houseeBay
RatingN/A

We're including a bonus curiosity because it's just too interesting not to mention. When Wizards of the Coast realized they had accidentally printed too many Base Set booster packs branded with the first-edition logo, they covered the errant symbol with a small black triangle. A simple attempt to avoid wasting resources has generated a much-prized collector's item, as fans now clamor for a rare Black Triangle Base Set Booster Pack.

It's the packaging itself that's valuable here, not the cards inside, so don't go cracking one of these black triangle packs open if you happen to find one sitting in the back of a drawer (you lucky devil).

They're occasionally found in standard Base Set booster boxes - so if you have one you'll have to weigh up whether to gamble on the chance discovery of one of the black triangle booster packs, or whether it's best to leave the box unopened for its pristine value. Some of the black triangle boosters have fetched over $2,700 (£2,000) on eBay, depending upon their condition and which Pokémon is displayed on their cover.

Rare Pokémon cards FAQ

How we find the most expensive Pokémon cards

To compile this list, we come back each month to trawl the latest sales on global trading card and collectibles auction houses like Fanatics Collect (formerly PWCC), Heritage Auctions, and Goldin Auctions. We aim to keep the rankings and prices as up to date as possible.

Remember that, like all collectibles and investments, the Pokémon card market is very volatile, and prices can change fast and often. If you're looking to buy and sell high value Pokémon cards, you need to take care to double check the latest prices, being very conscious of the website or auction house's commission rates and fees.

Which Pokémon cards are rarest?

The most valuable Pokémon cards normally command high prices because they're old and there are very few copies in circulation. Most originate from the earliest Pokémon sets, or are one-off tournament prize cards printed in very low numbers. First edition Pokémon cards, peculiar misprints, and desirable old promos all fetch very high prices.

How to tell if a Pokémon card is rare?

Wargamer has a dedicated guide to Pokémon card rarity covering the basic rarity levels of cards you can open in any pack. If you think an old card you've gotten hold of could be particularly valuable, our guides to first edition Pokémon cards and shadowless Pokémon cards will help you to identify them. It's also worth referring to our guide to fake Pokémon cards, as there are plenty of counterfeits on the market.

How to sell rare Pokémon cards

We have a dedicated guide on how to sell Pokémon cards, so we recommend you read that if you're considering trading - but here's the short version.

If you think you're holding a truly valuable Pokémon card, your first port of call is to get it protected by placing it in a thin, soft-plastic sleeve, then into a protective, hard-plastic 'toploader' case. Before spending any more money on the card, it's usually a good idea to show it to an expert in-person, to get their opinion on its condition and potential value. A specialist at your local games store may be able to help.

Then you should get it graded by a well-regarded, expert grading service - PSA Pokémon card grading is the most popular in the USA. Once you get the card back with an official grading from 1 to 10, and stored in a professional PSA protective case, you should have a good idea what price range you're likely to get for it.

Bear in mind that there's usually a huge difference in value between a PSA grade 7, 8, or 9 card (generally mint condition to the naked eye) and a perfect PSA 10 card (absolutely faultless, even when viewed under a microscope from every angle). The really high prices paid by top level collectors are only for PSA 10 cards, and a PSA 10 is very often worth more than twice as much as the exact same card at PSA grade 8 or 9.

If you don't find any ultra-valuable Pokémon cards in your collection, it's really not the end of the world. This is a game, remember - what you have got is a delightful collection to treasure and play with. If you want to share any new pack pulls or treasured classics with a community of fellow fans, you're most welcome in the Wargamer Discord!

To keep up to date with the latest news about new rare cards and any bargains we find, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: Kings of War: Assembling Your Forces (of Nature), Part 3
content:
G’day Tabletop Battles Readers! Welcome back to the third part of this series, focusing on building a Force of Nature army for Kings of War. If you’re not up to date, you can check out part two here. I’ve gotten quite a bit done since last time, so read on and see!

Painting Ydrin’s Company

Last time, I had the whole Champions box primed and had drybrushed the zenithal highlighting on, and was just about ready to start with the colours. I had one test model planned and painted, and I was on such a roll, went ahead with the rest of the unit.

The Swift Shots. Credit: Urr

On the whole, they were very fun to paint, and not hard to get up to a good standard, even when trying to go quickly. They have the right amount of detail to look good, and take the paint easily, without the need to paint many different decorative bits across the whole unit. I did find a few mould lines I had missed, but none in any important places.

I decided to keep a natural feeling paint scheme, with a lot of different browns and muted colours for the cloth. I’ve avoided metallics where I can as well, only the decorative earrings have any shine on these guys. Some of the weapons on the rest of the models will be metallic, but I’m thinking of it as a status symbol, so none for the slingers.

While I’ve kept the colours rather muted, I've played around with the browns. I’ve tried to keep all the models from becoming brown blobs, and kept the brown parts visually distinct. I’ve stuck with Citadels Snakebite Leather contrast paint across all the units’ leather equipment, slings, belt, straps etc. while switching between a few other browns for the wood that is on the models. Hopefully, the units across the army wouldn’t look like they’re in a uniform, but will still look cohesive as a whole.

Warriors of the Oak and Ash. Credit: Urr

I do think I went a little desaturated on some of the highlights, particularly on the cloth on the Swift Shots. These were the first unit I did, so I took that into consideration for the next units, and tried to keep things a little brighter.

After finishing the infantry, I just kept on going, rolling right into the Centaurs. It's been years since I've painted a horse, so I took inspiration from our own How to Paint Horses article. I adapted the infantry’s colour palette to the Centaurs, and matched it quite easily. So far, the units definitely have a cohesive design, and it makes it very easy to stick to a palette and style.

Painting Ydrin

I had more painting time this month than I thought, so as a reward to myself for finishing the rest of the Champions box, I finished Ydrin. I took the lessons from the rest of the infantry on board, and I’ve brightened him up in comparison. As most people do with their heroes, I've put a lot more work into him, even doing the eyes, which I usually never do. He was surprisingly quick to actually finish, as there’s not a whole lot of stuff actually on him, 90% of the model is wooden armour, flesh, leather and cloth, with no extra bits and bobs to painstakingly pick out.

He was a fun little project, and I’m very happy how he turned out. Hopefully he’ll be on the board soon.

Ydrin's Company. Credit: Urr

Finishing the Bases

As you can see above, I've also finalised how the bases will look, which I am also very happy with. There is a bit of work to do for them, but nothing too crazy.

They are done with a mix of Vallejo diorama FX Russian Mud and AK Terrains diorama series Dark Earth, slopped on the bases all over. I do this after adding the rocks I printed and painted, to make sure all the nooks and crannies are filled in. Some parts are left purely as one of the texture paints, but mostly they are mixed while still wet. This gives a differing colour gradient and texture mix across the bases. Once dry, I give it a black wash, and once that is dry, a drybrush of Vallejo Game Colours’ Beastly Brown. Then I add a variety of different tufts to the base. I’ve got three different manufacturers and six different styles for variety. Once they’re on, it’s snow time! This was the trickiest to get right, hence all the test bases. I’m using Green Stuff World’s Terrain Series Snow Powder. It works great once you read the tutorial on how to use it.

Building a Battalion

On top of all the painting and basing, I have been building. Mantic very kindly sent us the Forces of Nature Battalion box, and it is full of models! 50 of the Feraun infantry, eight Centaurs, three Earth Elementals and a Gladewalker Druid. The Feraun and Centaurs are the same sprues as in the Champions box, so they can be built into any of the units you are after.

I've switched it up and built half the Centaurs as the ranged version, and there's so much infantry, I've built some of everything.

Forces of Nature Battalion. Credit: Urr

On the back of all this building, I’ve been thinking about what I actually want to have done and ready to take to Clash Aus.

I’ve come up with this as a goal list (among many others):

1 x Chieftain

1 x Druid - Bane Chant (2), Heal (4)



1 x Centaur Chief - Banner of Command



2 x Tribal Warriors Horde - Spears



3 x Critters Troop



2 x Centaur Bray Striders Regiment - Sir Jesse’s Boots of Striding



1 x Grymbrocks Regiment



1 x Beast of Nature



2 x Guardian Brutes Regiment - Blessing of the Gods

Theoretically, I’ve got the hammers, anvils and chaff I like, but no shooting puts me a little on edge. There’s a few points floating for items, and wiggle room around all of this. You’ll note I have not built or painted essentially any of this, so there’s a very large amount of work to go. I don’t want to lock myself into too much of this, as Arrogance is coming out very shortly, and promises to shake up the whole game, but at least I have a goal!

So, with that hefty list of models to go, where does that leave me? Well, with a lot more building and painting to go! And even some games! Just in time for Arrogance to come out and throw it all up in the air. More on that shortly...

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: The rarest and most expensive Lorcana cards of 2026
content:
What are the rarest, most expensive Lorcana cards? When the characters and films are so beloved by so many, it only makes sense mega-fans are prepared to shell out for a rare Disney card with unique art of their favorite character. This guide covers all the most expensive Disney Lorcana card sales from the most recent sets.

Disney Lorcana may be the newest of the big trading card games, but it has a dedicated fanbase of collectors who will pay a princess' ransom to get their hands on the most coveted cards. Older TCGs may have higher price ceilings - nothing on this list can match the most expensive rare Pokémon cards or expensive Yugioh Cards - but there are some very valuable cards nonetheless! The most expensive Lorcana cards are:

Elsa, Spirit of Winter (Enchanted) - $942

The original Elsa from 2023's The First Chapter set is already a collectible card, but this full art Enchanted variant is in another league. She's a double threat - not just one of the most popular Disney characters of all time, but the first card printed of that character when the game launched. If you've got one, don't let it go…

Cinderella, Unintentional Icon (Iconic) - $1,004

Yes, she's serving. Released in October as part of Hyperia City, Cinderella's highest sale was a cool $1,500. We can understand why she's running behind set-companion Mickey Mouse - Best in Town, thanks to that more dynamic art, but this is no mean performance.

Hades, Looking for a Deal (Iconic) - $1,047

This is currently the rarest Disney villain card around! Though released alongside the previous Pocahontas in winterwear, and just as rare, this card took a lot longer to rise to the heights. Maybe it's because Hades isn't a princess? Still, this sneaky backstabber spent all of August closing the distance, and finally overtook her just before the month ended, capping out at a high of $1,200 in September.

Moana, Curious Explorer (Iconic) - $1,248

Moana was a surprise appearance in Winterspell, a set with a Winter theme, and it seems this explorer's curiosity is so great she didn't have time to dress for the colder weather. Nevertheless, this paper-cut inspired artwork is absolutely adorable, and helps to make this Iconic card so legendary.

Lilo and Stitch, Fun-Loving Friends (Iconic) - $1,497

There's so much energy and mischief in this Lilo and Stitch card. It looks like the box art for a straight-to-DVD sequel to the classic movie, and we mean that with love: there's no way any actual animation could live up to the sheer action this promises!

Ariel, Ethereal Voice (Iconic) - $1,537

This ghostly 'Whisper' of Ariel from the Whispers in the Well set not only has a commanding performance, she also commands a high price on the secondary market, which has only crept up since she released - the last sale, in September, hit $1,550.

Merida - Formidable Archer (Iconic) - $1,553

We all know that Lorcana is a pacifist game, and nobody involved in a challenge is ever hurt - but we have to wonder what Merida does with her arrows to keep her opponents from getting hurt! This is one of the most dynamic princes poses in all of Lorcana. While TCG player's market price is high, recent sales have all been far lower, around $900.

Winnie the Pooh, Hunny Wizard (Enchanted) - $1,598

The colors here are making us so hungry. Pooh Bear doesn't have any fancy abilities to show off, but he does have a soothing smile, a fancy cloak, and golden, sugary goodness surrounding him. Those base stats aren't too shabby, either. By the end of August, Winnie the Pooh was getting close to Ariel, after a long time jockeying for position with Moana.

Belle and Beast, Certain as the Sun (Iconic) - $1,725

A card as romantic as this was destined to be sought after - Belle and Beast waltzing is a timeless scene from the film that kicked off the Disney Renaissance.  They're also remarkably faithful to their original on-screen appearance as well. After dipping in September, the market valuation is back close to its original $2,000 mark.

Mickey Mouse - Best in Town (Iconic) - $1,871

Of course a new Mickey Mouse would sell like hot cakes - or hot dogs, as this jaunty take on the many-skilled rodent shows. Hyperia City only became available in October so this card is still being opened, but early sales have all clustered around that $2,000 mark. Time will tell if this is his high water mark, or merely the beginning.

Minnie Mouse, Sweetheart Princess (Iconic) - $3,093

When the first Iconic cards were created for Lorcana they were immediately way pricier than anything else on the market, and nearly made it into the all-time top 10, up against extremely rare early promos. Minnie, blowing a kiss in her medieval princess garb, was beginning to slip from her initial high position on the list - but made a recovery in late August as a sheer lack of supply drove up the market price. By October, she was back with a vengeance, with a high sale of $4,200 that's higher than Mickey has ever sold for!

Buzz Lightyear, Jungle Ranger (Iconic) - $3,616

When Wilds Unknown released Buzz Lightyear quickly became the second most valuable card you can open in a booster pack, topping out at $5,700 for a copy. Sales tailed off in June but it's had a few $3,600 sales since then, and it seems that's where it's stabilized.

Elsa, Ice Maker (Foil) - $3,979

Elsa cards always soar in price, and this Ice Maker is no different. The foil promo was available at various Challenge Season 2 Events in 2026, awarded to players who made the top 32. That means copies are pretty scarce, and some have sold for as high as $6,700, according to TCGPlayer. Given how new this card is, though, we're expecting its market price to fluctuate a little more before it settles.

Mickey Mouse, Brave Little Prince (Iconic) - $4,166

A copy of Mickey hasn't sold since July, so TCG Player's market valuation of $3,875 is very much an extrapolation from the last time the card moved and what would happen if one were to go on sale again. A sudden flurry of movement could result in Mickey being tipped from the top spot, or confirmed in his crown.

If you're a Lorcana collector but not yet a player, you should fix that immediately! It's easy to learn, and we can talk you through which Lorcana starter decks are worth playing.

title: The 29 most expensive Yugioh cards in 2026
content:
What are the most expensive Yugioh cards? Since the card game launched in 1999, collectors of rare YuGiOh cards have paid millions of dollars to get their hands on historic, storied, and unique cards. This guide profiles the 29 most expensive Yugioh cards ever, with the highest price they've sold for - and we've verified them all.

Before we start talking money, here's another guide of hideously pricey cards to check out: the most expensive rare Pokémon cards. Or, if you want to stick to Yugioh, here's the latest Yugioh banlist update.

The most expensive Yugioh cards ever sold are:

  • Tyler the Great Warrior
  • Alt Art Gemini Elf T3 04
  • Masahiro the Dark Clown Tournament Prize
  • Blue Eyes White Dragon LOB 1st Edition
  • Crush Card Virus Shonen Jump Championship 2007
  • Minerva, the Exalted Lightsworn 2015 Prize Card
  • Cyber Dragon GX Toy Promo
  • Cyber Stein Shonen Jump Championship 2004
  • KC Grand Tournament 2nd Place Dark Magician
  • Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth Dark Duel Stories Promo
  • The Seal of Orichalcos UDE Event
  • Blue Eyes White Dragon Dark Duel Stories Promo
  • Chaos Emperor, the Dragon of Armageddon Prize Card
  • Dark Magician LOB 1st Edition
  • Card of Sanctity Kids WB Promo
  • Doomcaliber Knight Shonen Jump Championship 2008
  • Morphing Jar Tournament Pack 2 Promo
  • Corrected Art Dark Paladin 1st Edition
  • German Pharaoh's Tour Prize Gold Sarcophagus
  • Dark Magician Girl 1st Edition
  • TG Hyper Librarian
  • Red Eyes Black Dragon LOB 1st Edition
  • Number 89: Diablosis the Mind Hacker Championship 2017
  • Gaia the Dragon Champion 1st Edition
  • Blue Eyes Shining Dragon Retro Pack 2
  • Gladiator's Assault Magic Formula
  • Exodia Legend Of Blue Eyes White Dragon 1st Edition
  • Attack of the Giant Card Cyber Dragon
  • Stainless Steel Black Luster Soldier

Tyler the Great Warrior

Worth $311,211

The most expensive Yugioh card of all time is Tyler the Great Warrior, a one-of-a-kind card designed by a 14-year-old, which sold for over $300k.

The card, created by Tyler Gressle in 2005 as part of a Make-a-Wish request, is the rarest Yugioh card in existence - there is only one copy in the world. Gressle designed the card in 2005, when he was 14, and battling against a rare form of liver cancer.

18 years later, he decided to sell the card. The final auction bid racked up a whopping $311,211 (£249,793.51), meaning yes, this is officially the rarest and most expensive Yugioh card ever, period.

This valuable card is a wonderful memento of the Make-a-Wish Foundation's work, as well as Tyler's own journey. We don't judge Tyler for selling the card - medical bills are very real, and perhaps he wanted to move on from that stage of his life - but we can't imagine owning it. It feels a bit strange to know that such a sentimental card is stowed away in a stranger's private collection.

Alt Art Gemini Elf T3-04

Worth $254,791

Back in 1999, Gemini Elf was the best level-four normal monster around thanks to its 1900 attack value, making it a landmark card in early Yugioh. That's likely why the 2001 Asian Championships featured the Alternate Artwork Gemini Elf T3-04 as its fourth-place prize card.

The Asian Championships tournament was held in Japan and only open to players in the Asian nations that had access to the OCG - remember, this was a year before the Trading Card Game was released in North America and the rest of the world. All five prize cards featured alternate artwork, a first for the game.

This version of Gemini Elf is rare and has plenty of historical value. It, and all the other prize cards, were presented to players by Kazuki Takahashi, the creator of Yugioh himself.

On May 8, 2024, trading card seller Vintage Card Japan announced via Twitter that it had sold a copy of the card privately for 40 million yen, roughly $254,791 by the exchange rate at the time. It's still only a Gemini Elf, but it's the most storied Gemini Elf ever printed.

Masahiro the Dark Clown Tournament Prize

Worth $173,923

Masahiro the Dark Clown is a quirky card with a strange history. It's one of three prize cards from Japan's 2001 Second National Tournament. The first, second, and third place winners were all awarded with a custom card featuring their literal face - and this strange anime monstrosity was born.

Kevin Tevart, US head of development for Yugioh, stated in a 2010 forum discussion that another one of the custom cards, Yasushi the Skull Knight, was a fake, adding "people will believe anything they read on a Wiki". But the card was on the Restricted List for the OCG's 2010 World Championship Series, hinting at its authenticity.

Further authenticating the card is PSA, who seems to have graded exactly one copy. Presumably, it's this one that sold on eBay for almost $174,000 in September 2025.

Blue-Eyes White Dragon LOB 1st Edition

Worth $85,000

Blue-Eyes White Dragon might be the most popular Yugioh card of all time, even if it isn't the rarest. A heavyweight both in the early days of the trading card game and the original anime series, it's still sought after today, especially if it's an ultra-rare mint-condition copy, like the Blue-Eyes White Dragon LOB 1st Edition.

Released in the game's first expansion set, Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon (LOB), this first-edition PSA 10 Gem Mint condition card sold at auction in October 2020 for an astounding $85,000 (£65,000).

Such rare copies don't always reach that lofty height. In September 2023, another Gem Mint 10 copy sold on auction house Goldins for $28,000, plus $5,600 buyer's premium - a comparative bargain.

This isn't the only valuable Blue-Eyes printing. Back in June 2021, a Chinese court suspended an auction after bidding spiraled up to a wild $13.4 million / £10.1 million, as people clambered to get their hands on an ultra-rare Blue-Eyes White Dragon with a 20th-anniversary card frame.

Crush Card Virus Shonen Jump Championship 2007

Worth $50,000

As the name implies, the Crush Card Virus Shonen Jump Championship 2007 was a prize card from a tournament that pre-dated (and was later replaced by) the Yugioh Championship Series. Originally, 40 copies of this rare Yugioh card were produced, before a further two were made for the SJC 2008 tournaments.

It's the scarcity of this card that makes it so valuable to collectors, more so than its functionality or popularity. In June 2020, a PSA 10 gem mint copy sold for $49,999 (£40,058.70) on eBay. Not bad for a card that spent most of its life sitting on the Yugioh banlist, before Konami rewrote its rules text.

Minerva, the Exalted Lightsworn 2015 Prize Card

Worth $34,800

An ultra-rare variant of Minerva, The Exalted Lightsworn was awarded as the first prize in national heats for the 2015 Yugioh World Championship Series. The distinction between this version and the cards given out for second and third place is very subtle: the golden lettering is all that separates it from its kindred.

One such card with an excellent condition score of 9.5 sold via Heritage Auctions on November 6 2021 for $34,800, followed in March 2022 by a 9.0 condition card that moved for $31,200. Minerva might not matter much in the meta these days, but this card remains iconic.

Cyber Dragon GX Toy Promo

Worth $30,500

Back when the GX anime first aired on American TV, Konami partnered up with toy maker Mattel to release a range of action figures. Available only from Sears stores, each toy was a popular Yugioh summon, and the packs came with a limited edition version of that monster's card. However, midway through the third series of toys, the accompanying 'MF03' series of cards was pulled from the product.

This meant that cards for monsters released towards the end of the run had particularly short supply, none more so than MF03-009 Cyber Dragon. For many years this promo card was practically a myth: although it was listed in official guides to published cards, there were no photos of it in the wild.

That was until 2020, when redditor loserchris (real name Kevin, no surname given) shared the news on the r/yugioh subreddit that he had found several MF03 series cards in his closet, saying "I don't even remember where I got them". The community was flabbergasted that an MF03-009 was tucked among them.

Kevin sold the Cyber Dragon via an auction on the YGOrganization Discord, and confirmed to Wargamer that he received a tidy $30,500 for the card.

Cyber-Stein Shonen Jump Championship 2004

Worth $30,100

This copy of Cyber-Stein was originally awarded as a prize card at the Shonen Jump Championships between 2004 and 2005. Only 18 copies of the valuable card were produced for the tournaments, although an extra two were printed for the tournaments in 2008, and 126 copies were made for a promotional event in 2009.

Regardless of its reprints, this is still a rare Yugioh card. A PSA 10 gem mint condition copy printed in the original 2004 auctioned in October 2020 for $30,100 (£22,800).

KC Grand Tournament 2nd Place Dark Magician

Worth $30,000

During the Coronavirus pandemic, Konami wisely suspended the World Championship for its mobile game Yugioh Duel Links, and in 2020 to 2022 it hosted the purely digital Kaiba Corporation Grand Tournament as a replacement. The prizes for the 2021 championship were trophy blocks containing Ultra Secret Rare printings of Dark Magician, which have no foiling on the Wizard's robes.

2021's second place finalist didn't hang onto their card for long, selling it via Heritage Auctions on December 2, 2022, where it sold for $32,000 plus $6,400 buyer's premium. The same card sold again via the same auction house almost exactly two years later, this time only hitting $30,000 (plus a larger $7,500 buyer's premium) on December 6 2024.

Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth Dark Duel Stories Promo

Worth $30,000

This little insect doesn't have much renown in the TCG community, but Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth made a name for itself as a valuable Yugioh card in August 2021. That's when a rare promo version of the card, released alongside the Dark Duels Stories Game Boy cartridge, with a PSA 10 gem mint rating sold on eBay for a whopping $29,999.99 (£22,700).

At the time of its listing, it was billed as the only gem mint copy of the promo card in the entire world. Since then, trading card authenticator and grading company PSA has listed three other copies of the card.

The Seal of Orichalcos UDE Event

Worth $26,400

The Seal of Orichalcos has appeared in several Yugioh sets, but not until years after it had debuted in the fourth season of the Yugioh anime. Upper Deck Entertainment decided to make their own custom version of the card.

This rare Yugioh card appeared only in UDE-organised "Duel the Master" side-events at tournaments. These were challenge games played against a master player, usually a judge, who wielded a stacked deck full of powerful cards.

The Seal of Orichalcos isn't really a promo, since it wasn't intended to make its way into the hands of players, and was never legal in any form of tournament play. This version of the card has an ominous final clause - if you lose against its owner, your soul is forfeit! Legend has it that only fifteen copies of the card were ever printed, suggesting it is one of the rarest cards in any TCG.

In 2017, Yu-Gi-Oh! collector Anthony Nguyen released a YouTube video revealing he'd acquired a copy of the legendary card. Once it became apparent that it was possible for collectors to get their hands on it, there were a spate of sales - with a 7-graded copy selling via Heritage Auctions for $26,400.

Blue-Eyes White Dragon Dark Duel Stories Promo

Worth $25,100

Another entry for the pallid serpent, this was one of six Prismatic Secret Rare cards released as a promotion for the Yugioh Dark Duel Stories Gameboy game. Opening the game box would reveal one of two different sets of cards, one containing ol' Blue-Eyes White Dragon, Exodia, and Dark Magician; the other contained Acid Trap Hole, Seiyaryu, Salamandra, and a sense of crushing disappointment.

This PSA 10 gem mint condition copy sold at auction in February 2021 for the not-insignificant sum of $25,100 (£19,000). Although a fair few prismatic Blue-Eyes White Dragons made their way into the world as promo cards for the videogame, few have been kept in such great condition.

Chaos Emperor, the Dragon of Armageddon Prize Card

Worth $18,000

Chaos Emperor, the Dragon of Armageddon was a prize in the 2018 Yugioh Championship series. Championship winners were the first to get their hands on the powerful dragon, two years before its was available to the rest of the world in Battles of Legend Armageddon.

While it requires a lot of reading, this expensive Yugioh card has some pretty explosive effects. You can wipe out your opponent's board and their life points with its unique monster effect, or play it to either pendulum zone to retrieve another dragon from your graveyard. A copy of the ultra-rare first-place winner's card with a PSA Mint 9 rating sold via Heritage auctions for $18,000 in November 2021.

Dark Magician LOB 1st Edition

Worth $17,924

Another staple of the Yugioh anime and trading card game, Dark Magician is best known as the favorite card of protagonist Yugi Muto. And with that fame comes expense. Aa PSA 10 gem mint condition Dark Magician LOB 1st Edition, printed in the Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon set, was auctioned in July 2021 for $17,924 (£14,163).

Supposedly, the price of this card can climb even higher. Dicebreaker reported that, in June 2021, an Arkana variant (with a red background behind the magician) sold on eBay for a whopping $85,000. However, we've not seen a sale since then that's come anywhere close to such a price - though almost $20,000 for a single card is still eye-watering.

Card of Sanctity Kids WB Promo

Worth $17,000

This very valuable Yugioh card went for $17,000 plus buyer's premium on the auction site Goldin in April 2024. It's a special promo card that was given away by Kids WB in a tie-in with the Yugioh anime. The episode 'Back to Battle City Part 3' included instructions for US kids to enter a sweepstakes, and 100 winners received this special Card of Sanctity.

Naturally those priceless prizes were stuffed into drawers, traded away on the playground, bent, torn, or left outside in the rain. The $17,000 copy that sold at Goldins only has a PSA 8 Near Mint grade: there are basically no higher-quality versions of the card available.

It's worth noting that this card is a lot less powerful than the version in the anime, where it made each player draw up to six cards in their hand.

Doomcaliber Knight Shonen Jump Championship 2008

Worth $15,300

This copy of Doomcaliber Knight was handed to winners of the 2008 Shonen Jump Championships. Only 68 copies of the cards were ever produced.

In March 2021, a PSA 7 near-mint copy of the card was auctioned for $15,300 (£12,258.21). This is one of very few cards on this list that isn't graded PSA 10 - and since a copy has never been sold in PSA 10 condition, it's hard to know if they exist at all. The fact that copies sell for such high prices without a perfect grading goes to show how valuable the card is.

Morphing Jar Tournament Pack 2 Promo

Worth $15,000

Another promotional card, this copy of Morphing Jar was released in the second season Tournament Pack, a specially-compiled booster that was released at select tournament locations in late 2002. More than that, Morphing Jar was the pack's single Ultra Rare, making it doubly golden - and a pretty valuable card on the secondary market.

In Early 2021, a PSA 10 gem mint condition copy of the card sold for just under $15,000 (£12,000). Though we still think that Pot of Greed is the best piece of crockery to ever make its way into Yugioh.

Corrected Art Dark Paladin 1st Edition

Worth $15,000

Often, when a trading card gets misprinted, its recipient's dismay turns to glee when they realize their misshapen playing piece is now a rare collector's item. But in the case of Dark Paladin, it's the 'correction' to that misprint that now holds immense value.

The first edition English printing of Dark Paladin from the 2003 Yugioh set Magician's Force used the incorrect artwork. Upper Deck Entertainment, the distributor for English-language Yugioh cards in the 2000s, corrected the mistake for later editions of the card. But it also offered players with the misprinted card a chance to swap their 1st edition Dark Paladins for 1st edition Dark Paladins with the corrected art.

The offer was advertised on Upper Deck's website, and in various magazines. But it seems like many fans either didn't hear about it, didn't bother to send off for the card, or thought the misprint would be more valuable in the long run. Very few copies were put into circulation - and now the corrected art version of the Dark Paladin is much rarer and more expensive.

The highest recent price we could find was a PSA-graded gem mint condition copy that sold for $15,000 on Fanatics Collect on May 11, 2021. Props go to the Reddit user AzulRyu who documented this bit of TCG history in exhaustive detail.

German Pharaoh's Tour Prize Gold Sarcophagus

Worth $14,999

Another championship prize card, Gold Sarcophagus was the prize for national winners in the 2007 Pharoah's Tour series. The Ultra-Rare variant was awarded to first-place winners. Copies are extremely scarce, and this PSA 9-graded copy that sold in October 2025 is the only known copy of this grading.

Dark Magician Girl 1st Edition

Worth $13,200

Dark Magician Girl was first printed in 2003, in the North-America only set Magician's Force. Although she's had a wider reprint since then, this was the only printing to feature the card art used in the Yugioh anime.

A gem mint first edition Dark Magician girl sold for $9,100 via eBay in November 2020, while another sold for $13,200 via PWCC marketplace in July 2022. The deck archetype this expensive Yugioh card belongs to no longer sees much success at tournaments, but its rarity and the iconic status of the card keep its value high.

T.G. Hyper Librarian

Worth $11,250

Another tournament prize card, T.G. Hyper Librarian was given out as an exclusive never-before-seen card in 2011 to those who qualified in the National Championships to go on and take part in the World Championship series.

As that year's World Championships had 26 participants, that means that only 26 copies of this card were made. T.G. Hyper Librarian would only be a mechanically exclusive card for a year, as it got a wider printing in the 2012 set Return of the Duelist Special Edition. But that didn't quash the value of the original prize cards: a PSA 10 copy fetched $11,250 on Heritage Auctions in December 2024.

Red-Eyes Black Dragon LOB 1st Edition

Worth $10,600

Another favorite from Yugioh's line of vivid drakes with notable eye colors, Red-Eyes Black Dragon doesn't have the acclaim or market value of its esteemed Blue-eyed counterpart, but can certainly hold its own. One of ten Ultra Rares included in the first Yugioh set release, Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon, this card was a prize to find.

Twenty years later, that prize has only gone up in value. A PSA 10 gem mint condition copy of the first-edition card cards for $10,600 (£8,000) in January 2021. Yugioh players sure do like their dragons.

Number 89: Diablosis the Mind Hacker Championship 2017

Worth $10,500

Number 89: Diablosis the Mindhacker was an exclusive card given to Yugioh Championship Series winners in 2017. The average duellist then had to wait four years for it to get a regular release in the 2021 set Brothers of Legend.

Most valuable Yugioh cards are rare but not powerful, but Diablosis is both. Its ability to banish cards from the opponent's extra deck, graveyard, and the top of their deck made it a disrupting terror in recent times, forcing many players to warp their deck-building process in an effort to counter it.

Fortunately, the aggrieved fans' prayers were answered when, in June 2023, the card was stuck onto the Yugioh banlist. It found its way to the Yugioh Master Duel banlist soon afterwards, in October.

Getting plenty of play will probably have boosted its market value at least a little, but ultimately it's the low supply, inherent to any prize card, that has made Diablosis so expensive. According to Heritage Auctions, which oversaw the sale of a copy for $10,500 in September 2022, only nine PSA 10 copies are known to exist.

Gaia the Dragon Champion 1st Edition

Worth $9,900

One of only two Secret Rare cards released in the very first Yugioh set, Gaia the Dragon Champion depicts a terrifying fusion between Gaia the Fierce Knight and Curse of Dragon. Terrifying in appearance, that is; with no abilities and mediocre stats, this warrior wouldn't stand a chance in the modern TCG meta.

You might think being one of the two rarest cards in the earliest Yugioh set would be enough to explain Gaia's high price, with a copy selling on Heritage Auctions for $9,9000 in 2021. However, the other Secret Rare card from the set, Tri-Horned Dragon, commands a pitiful price in comparison, of just a few hundred dollars.

Just like other more common and yet more expensive Legend of Blue Eyes cards such as Dark Magician and Blue-Eyes itself, it seems it is prestige that accounts for the difference. Gaia the Dragon Champion is a far more popular card than Tri-Horned Dragon, appearing in the anime's fifth episode, getting more reprints and appearing in more video games than its less appealing horny lizard friend.

Blue-Eyes Shining Dragon Retro Pack 2

Worth $9,000

Blue-Eyes Shining Dragon is one of nine Secret Rares from Retro Pack 2, with a bit of extra prestige thanks to the Blue-Eyes connection. The original limited edition printing of this card was given to kids who saw the 2004 movie, Yugioh: Pyramid of Light, in theaters. But it's actually this unlimited reprint from a few years later (2009) that's most expensive.

That's because, even though it's 'just' a reprint set, Retro Pack 2 had an extremely low print run and was very hard to get hold of in America. Boxes were released only in Europe, and now easily sell for over $5,000.

Less perfect copies of this exact card can be found online for $1000 - $2000, but the most staggering sale we found was a PSA 10 Gem Mint specimen that sold via Fanatics Collect in February 2021 for $9,000.

There's a funny bit of trivia about this card. You have to tribute Blue-Eyes Ultimate Dragon to summon Blue-Eyes Shining Dragon - but the Ultimate Dragon wasn't released until almost two years after the Shining Dragons's first printing, meaning this iconic dragon was completely unusable! D'oh!

Gladiator's Assault Magic Formula

Worth $8,700

When Magic Formula was printed in the 2007 set Gladiator's Assault, it became a key part of Dark Magician decks, offering power boosts to either Dark Magician or Dark Magician Girl, and a handy life boost should it go to the graveyard. The problem for duellists was getting their hands on it.

Gladiator's Assault was stuffed with secret rare cards and had a legendarily bad ratio of rare cards to commons and uncommons. Magic Formula was incredibly scarce, and copies from that first printing are still highly sought after: a gem mint Gladiator's Assault Magic Formula sold for $8,700 on PWCC marketplace in July 2022.

Exodia Legend Of Blue Eyes White Dragon 1st Edition

Worth $8,000

The notorious Exodia is just as prized on the collector's market as it is by duelists in the Yugioh anime. It's the ultimate monster, created by combining five Exodia cards into a single, unmatched entity: the Forbidden One. It's so powerful, in fact, that it grants its summoner immediate victory. No wonder that sniveling Weevil Underwood threw all of Yugi's Exodia cards off the boat in the first season.

This copy of Exodia is particularly prized for being a first-edition version that was printed in the game's original set from 2002, Legend of Blue-Eyes White Dragon. It sold for $8,000 (£6,050), thanks no doubt to being graded at PSA 10 Mint Gem condition.

Attack of the Giant Card!! Cyber Dragon

Price Unconfirmed

In addition to being one of the most expensive Yugioh cards ever sold, the Attack of the Giant Card!! Cyber Dragon is also one of the biggest. 'Attack of the Giant Card!!' is an official tournament that rewards its winner with a Yugioh card that's around a meter tall.

According to an eBay listing, this giant Cyber Dragon was awarded at the Remote Duel Extravaganza in June 2022 as part of the Attack of the Giant Card!! Speed Duel tournament. Though we don't know the official offer accepted, the seller's OG asking price was just under $10,000 (£9,000) - so the final price is somewhere in this eye-watering ballpark.

Stainless Steel Black Luster Soldier

Rumored to be worth millions

Believed to have been awarded in Yugioh's first-ever national tournament in 1999, this curious card might be the most expensive Yugioh card of all time. Made of stainless steel, the unique one-of-a-kind Black Luster Soldier monster works differently to every other version of the card - since it's a Normal Monster, not a Ritual Monster.

According to Kotaku, the card was listed for sale for around $10 million back in 2013, but there's no indication it sold for that value. Elsewhere, a figure of $2 million is widely circulated, but this does not seem to have a verifiable source attached.

The above image is not the metal monster, but a paper duplicate of the card. 3,000 copies were released in June 2023 as a special promotion in Japan, to mark the 25th anniversary of the game.

How we check Yugioh card prices

Our guide is based on the highest prices each rare Yugioh card has fetched in sales we can verify. Every month, we review the most recent verified sales at various major online auction houses for collectibles, such as Goldin Auctions, Fanatics Collect, and Heritage Auctions. If a new sale beats a record, it makes the list. We also trawl eBay listings, but these sales are much more difficult to verify, and we'll never list a card's sale value unless we're satisfied the details are completely accurate.

There are cards that have been offered at higher prices, like the Blue Eyes Ultimate Dragon from the 2001 Asian Championships, but these don't have verified sales. The one exception on our list is the Stainless Steel Black Luster Soldier: this has never been sold, but it is such a renowned card that if it ever went to auction it would certainly become one of the most expensive Yugioh cards of all time.

For more costly trading cards, check out our guides to the most expensive MTG cards, and the most expensive Lorcana cards in Disney's TCG.

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana Returns – Chaosium’s Definitive Mythos Guide Hits in October
content:
Chaosium is releasing a new fourth edition of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana this October, bringing the definitive guide to Lovecraftian horror back to shelves in full-color hardback format.

First published in 1994 and updated several times since, the book compiles detailed entries on mythos deities, creatures, tomes, and artifacts—from Azathoth to Zylac—tracing their appearances across fiction and pop culture. This new edition features updated text, evocative interior art, and a cover by John Sumrow, along with a fresh essay from author Dan Harms on the question “What is the Cthulhu Mythos?” Timelines of the Necronomicon, a cosmic horror bibliography, and illustrations of Nyarlathotep, Hastur, and Cthulhu himself round out the package.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).
